content.fi:
Vapaaehtoistoiminnassa toteutuvaa työelämäjaksoa (5 op) ohjaa kurssisivun linkin takaa löytyvä Moodle-verkkokurssi. Opiskelija kirjaa noin 40 tunnin vapaaehtoistyönsä osaksi oppimispäiväkirjaa, jonka hän palauttaa lopuksi kurssin opettajalle. Oppimispäiväkirjassa hän pohtii myös motivaatiotaan ja vapaaehtoistyön merkitystä hänelle mahdollisena tulevaisuuden työllistäjänä.

Opiskelija työskentelee tehtävässä, joihin hän voisi valmistuttuaan siirtyä tieteenalansa asiantuntijana, toimii yhteiskunnassa vastuullisesti ja laajentaa verkostoja tulevaisuuden työllistymistään varten. Opiskelija suunnittelee ja arvioi, millä olemassa olevilla ja uusilla tavoilla tieteenalakohtaista tietoa ja taitoa voi soveltaa eettisesti ja vastuullisesti järjestö- ja vapaaehtoistoiminnassa sekä millä tavoilla ne voisivat johtaa myös toimeentuloon ja työllistymiseen tai yrittäjyyteen.


Helsingin yliopiston hallinto- ja opiskelijajärjestötoimintaan osallistumisesta myönnettäviä opintopisteitä säätelee erillinen rehtorin päätös. Tämän opintojakson suoritusta ei voi myöntää hallinto- ja opiskelijajärjestötoiminnasta saatavilla opintopisteillä.

additional.en:
Target group

The component is open to bachelor’s students of the Faculty of Social Sciences. Certain methods of completing Organisational Activities and Volunteer Work are suited to both bachelor’s and master’s studies.


Timing

Third year of studies, periods 2–4.


Completion methods
  • Credits granted for organisational activities (not counted as work experience)
  • Credits granted for volunteer work (not counted as work experience)

Contents

The career module included in the degree requirements of the programme completed as Organisational Activities and Volunteer Work (5 cr) requires working in duties that could be completed by a recent graduate of the field. However, the working hours completed for the ‘employer’ are fewer than in a salaried position. Correspondingly, more time is dedicated to developing students’ skills in accordance with separately drawn up instructions. Through organisational activities and volunteer work, students will gain experience in working as experts in their field, work in the context of society and establish networks for future employment. Students will identify and plan ways in which discipline-specific knowhow can be applied to organisational activities and volunteer work, as well as how they could lead to a livelihood and employment. The component includes an initial and/or final assignment. A separate rector’s decision provides for credits granted for activities in the University’s administrative bodies and student organisations. The component can also be completed, for example, by participating in the activities of the Helsinki and Uusimaa District of the Finnish Red Cross. This completion method requires attendance in orientation (schedules to be separately announced).


Assessment practices and criteria

Self-assessment and possible assessment by the supervisor or coordinator of the organisational activities and volunteer work, and/or peer assessment.

The component is graded on a scale of pass/fail.


Other information

Degree programmes can also organise the course independently.


Responsible person

University lecturer Markku Sippola
additional.fi:
Toteutus

Opintojakso edellyttää toimintaa tehtävissä, jotka voisivat olla tieteenalalta valmistuneen työtehtäviä. ”Työnantajalle” tehtävä tuntimäärä on kuitenkin vähäisempi kuin työharjoittelussa eli vähintään 40h. Erikseen muotoiltavan ohjeistuksen mukaista opiskelijan osaamisen kehittämistä on vastaavasti enemmän.


Aiemman järjestö- ja vapaaehtoistoiminnan hyväksilukemisesta voi tiedustella tutkinto-ohjelman työelämäopettajalta.

Kohderyhmä

Opintojakso on avoin valtiotieteellisen tiedekunnan kandiopiskelijoille. Osa järjestö- ja vapaaehtoistoimintaan liittyvistä toteutuksista soveltuu sekä kandi- että maisteriopintoihin.
additional.sv:
Målgrupp

Studieavsnittet är öppet för kandidatstuderande vid Statsvetenskapliga fakulteten. En del av förenings- och frivilligverksamhetens alternativ lämpar sig för både kandidat- och magisterstudierna.


Timing

Tredje studieåret, 2–4 perioden


Studieavsnittets form
  • Studiepoäng för föreningsverksamhet (inte arbetserfarenhet)
  • Studiepoäng för frivilligverksamhet (inte arbetserfarenhet)

Innehåll

Om examensfordringarnas arbetslivsavsnitt genomförs i form av förenings- och frivilligverksamhet (5 sp) förutsätter det att studenten arbetar med uppgifter som skulle kunna skötas av en person med en examen inom vetenskapsområdet. Antalet arbetstimmar som utförs i ”arbetsgivarens” regi är dock färre än vid avlönat arbete. I stället betonas utvecklingen av studentens egen kompetens i enlighet med särskilt formulerade anvisningar. Genom förenings- och frivilligverksamheten får studenten erfarenhet av att arbeta som expert inom sitt vetenskapsområde, agerar i samhället och skapar nätverk med tanke på framtida sysselsättning. Studenten identifierar och planerar hur man kan tillämpa vetenskapsområdets kunskaper och färdigheter inom förenings- och frivilligverksamhet och hur det går att på det sättet försörja sig och få arbete. I studieavsnittet ingår en inledande uppgift och/eller en avslutande uppgift. Antalet studiepoäng som beviljas för deltagande i universitetets förvaltningsorgans och studentföreningarnas verksamhet regleras genom ett särskilt rektorsbeslut. Studieavsnittet kan också genomföras t.ex. vid Finlands Röda Kors Helsingfors och Nylands distrikt. Om studieavsnittet genomförs vid FRK krävs det att studenten deltar i en introduktion (tidpunkterna meddelas separat).


Bedömningsmetoder och kriterier

Självvärdering samt eventuell utvärdering från chefen eller den ansvarige för förenings- och frivilligverksamheten och/eller kamratutvärdering.

Studieavsnittet bedöms med vitsordet godkänt/underkänt.


Övrig information

Studieavsnittet kan också arrangeras som en egen kurs i ett utbildningsprograms regi.


Ansvarig person

Universitetslektor Markku Sippola

outcomes.en: Business Analytics refers to the use of quantitative models to help make better business decisions. This course focuses on mathematical optimization models that are commonly used in business applications. After the course the student can (i) recognize the types of real-world business decision problems where use of these models brings added value, (ii) interpret results of these models to derive defensible decision recommendations, and (iii) build and solve these models using relevant software to support business decision making.
outcomes.fi: Analytiikalla tarkoitetaan kvantitatiivisten mallien käyttöä päätöksenteon tukemisessa. Tämä kurssi keskittyy matemaattisen optimoinnin malleihin, joita käytetään yleisesti liiketoimintasovelluksissa. Kurssin jälkeen opiskelija kykenee (i) tunnistamaan liiketoiminnan päätöksentekotilanteita, joissa näiden mallien käyttö tuo lisäarvoa, (ii) tulkitsemaan näiden mallien tuloksia ja tekemään niiden pohjalta perusteltuja päätössuosituksia, sekä (iii) rakentamaan ja ratkaisemaan näitä malleja käyttäen sopivia tietokoneohjelmistoja päätöksenteon tukemiseksi.

prerequisites.en: Recommended prerequisites: The students are expected to have completed courses ISM-A1002 "Johdatus data-analytiikkaan" ("Introduction to data analytics") and 30A02000 "Tilastotieteen perusteet" ("Introduction to statistics"), or obtained equivalent skills from other university level courses. These skills include basics of linear algebra, multivariate functions, matrixes, vectors, probability, random variables as well as good Excel skills. Previous experience in programming with some modern language (Python, R, Java) will be useful.
prerequisites.fi: Suositellut esitiedot: Opiskelijoiden odotetaan suorittaneen kurssit ISM-A1002 "Johdatus data-analytiikkaan" ja 30A02000 "Tilastotieteen perusteet" tai hankkineen vastaavat taidot muilta yliopistotason kursseilta. Näihin taitoihin kuuluu perusteet lineaarialgebrasta, monimuuttujafunktioista, matriiseista, vektoreista, todennäköisyyslaskennasta, satunnaismuuttujista sekä hyvä Excelin käyttötaito. Aikaisempi kokemus ohjelmoinnista jollakin modernilla kielellä (Python, R, Java) on hyödyllistä.

LITO-opintokokonaisuudessa opintojaksot järjestetään yliopistojen välisenä yhteistyönä. Jotta opiskelijan opintosuoritus saadaan kirjattua, hänestä siirretään kotiyliopiston rekisteristä opetusta järjestävän yliopiston rekisteriin seuraavat tiedot: nimi, sukupuoli, sähköpostiosoite, kansalaisuus, henkilötunnus ja kotiyliopisto. outcomes.en: The student understands the concept of relativity of time and space, knows the basics of special relativity, in particular, the Lorentz transformation, and is able to apply it (both its basic and differential form) to problems. The student masters the generalization of Newton's law F=ma to special relativity, four vectors, and simple algebra with them (e.g. "dot product"). Schwarzschild's metrics and black holes become familiar from the theory of general relativity. From cosmology the student learns a few basic concepts.

prerequisites.en: BSMA1001 Linear algebra and complex numbers or similar knowledge on basic linear algebra, matrix and vector calculus, Taylor series, derivation and integration. (Also recommended BSPH1001 Interactions and bodies, BSPH1002 Matter and interactions.)

content.en:
A brief non-relativistic intro: Galilei transformation (universal time, but relative velocities).

The theory of special relativity: basics, the principle of relativity of both the time and spatial coordinates, Lorentz transformation, causality, summing up velocities (Galilei vs. special relativity), flagpole and twin paradoxes, Minkowski metrics, four-dimensional space-time, tensor formalism (mostly just four vectors and the metric tensor), generalization of Newton's laws, relativistic dynamics (basic laws, E = mc2, relativistic version of F=ma, Doppler phenomenon).

The theory of General Relativity: gravity as curvature of space-time, equivalence principle, non-Minkowski metrics, Schwarzchild metrics and black holes, gravitational redshift, gravitational lenses, gravitational waves.

Cosmology: The Big Bang, Friedmann-Robertson-Walker metrics and expanding Universe, dark matter and energy, cosmic microwave background radiation.

additional.en:
Completion methods

Weekly lectures, independent work (reading the course material, solving exercises), weekly exercises, which are solved partly in the workshop sessions with the help of assistants in small groups and partly independently. Exercises are returned to assistants who score them.

The course is graded on a scale from 0 to 5. When determining a grade, 2/3 of the points will become from the course exam and 1/3 of the points will be based on the exercises.

The course is conducted as a contact teaching (weekly lectures and exercise/workshop sessions), but attending the lectures is not compulsory. The course is passed either by returning exercises to be assessed and by course exam or alternatively by general exam.

Assessment practices and criteria

Grading scale is 0 (failed) - 1 (passed) - 5 (excellent)

Activities and methods in support of learning

Weekly lectures, independent work by the student, weekly exercise sessions, which are partly done in calculation workshops in small groups, and partly independently.

The exercise sessions are returned to the assistants, who score them. The total workload for the course is 135 hours.

Programme: Bachelor's programme in Science.

The course is lectured every other year, even years in period 4.

The course is recommended for the students of the Bachelor's programme in Science in the Physics study track in the 1st - 3rd year of studies.

Intermediate studies in physics

outcomes.en: Energy literacy. The course aims to give basic insights into energy economy, as well as qualitative understanding of wind, hydro, solar and nuclear power technologies as well as fossil-fueled plants.
outcomes.fi: Energialukutaito ja suuruusluokka-ajattelu: energiantuotantoon liittyvät peruskäsitteet; fossiilisiin polttoaineisiin, uusiutuviin energialähteisiin ja ydinvoimaan perustuvien teknologioiden kvalitatiivinen ymmärtäminen; sähköverkon merkitys; energiantuotantoon liittyvät riskit ja niiden vertailu sekä ilmaston että terveyden kannalta; tulevaisuuden lupaukset energia-alalla. Kurssi antaa pohjan teknisemmille energia-alaan liittyville kursseille (esim. ENY-C2002).

content.en: Outline of core contents 1. Key concepts: From energy production to energy use, and everything in between. 2. Electrifying Finland: Power production, transmission and consumption. 3. Energy and the economy: From electric currents to monetary flows. 4. Stoked up over energy: Fossil fuels. 5. Zero carbon emissions? Renewable sources of energy. 6. Splitting uranium: Basic facts about nuclear power. 7. Risk-free? Radiation, nuclear waste, Chernobyl, Fukushima. 8. Indoor heating going out the window? 9. Costs and benefits: Energy risks and their management. 10. Power reserves: Energy saving and storage. 11. Future sources of energy: Anything new on the horizon? 12. Presenting and reflecting on the conclusions of the student assignment.
content.fi: Runkohahmotelma: 1. Peruskäsitteet energiantuotannosta energiankäyttöön ja kaikki siltä väliltä; 2. Sähköinen Suomi: sähkön tuotanto, siirto ja kulutus; 3. Energia ja talous: sähkövirroista rahavirroiksi; 4. Ihan hiilenä energiasta: fossiiliset polttoaineet; 5. Hiilipäästöt kohti nollaa? Uusiutuvat energialähteet; 6. Uraani halkeaa: perusasiat ydinvoimasta; 7. Riskiä vailla? Säteily, ydinjäte, Tshernobyl ja Fukushima; 8. Lämpöä ihmisille vai harakoille?; 9. Hyötyjä ja haittoja: energiariskit ja niiden hallinta; 10. Sähköä säilömään: energian säästö ja varastointi; 11. Tulevaisuuden energialähteet - onko mitään uutta näköpiirissä?; 12. Seurantatehtävän johtopäätösten esittely ja pohdinta.
content.sv: Skiss över kursens struktur: 1: Grundbegrepp från energiproduktion till energianvändning och allt däremellan; 2. Det elektrifierade Finland: elproduktion, elöverföring och elkonsumtion; 3. Energi och ekonomi: från elström till pengaström; 4. Laddad av energi: Fossila bränslen; 5. Kolutsläppen mot noll? Förnybara energikällor; 6. Uranklyvning: grundfakta om kärnenergi; 7. Utan risk? Strålning, kärnavfall, Tjernobyl och Fukushima; 8. Värme för människorna eller kråkorna?; 9. Fördelar och nackdelar: risker med energi och hur de hanteras; 10. Att förvara el: energisparande och förvaring; 11. Framtidens energikällor – finns det något nytt i sikte?; 12. Presentation av uppföljningsuppgiftens slutsatser samt reflexion.

content.en:
An AI agent is a program that can perform tasks autonomously on behalf of a user or another program. One critical question is how AI agents interact with the ""real world"", where the real world refers to both humans and the broader physical environment. From the perspective of the AI agent, the real world is a complex environment. This complexity imposes constraints on the extent to which the environment can be taken into account in designing AI agents that perform specific tasks.
In this course we explore how AI agents can be designed to deal with the interface between code and the real world to reliably achieve desired goals. Concretely, in the course:

  • Students, in groups, will develop an idea into a concept or prototype of an AI agent that interacts with the real world
  • Doing so they will consider design, technology and business perspectives
  • At the end of the oucrse they will present their work to a broader audience

This course has been designed with a broad range of students in mind to get a mix of perspectives on designing and interacting with AI agents. Students will work in multidisciplinary teams, ideally including technology, design and business perspectives.

If you have taken Fourier analysis II, you cannot take Fourier Analysis and Distributions (5 cr) If you have taken Real Analysis II, you cannot take Advanced Course in Real Analysis (10 cr) If you have taken one of the courses: Real analysis I and Fourier analysis I ( and neither of the courses real analysis II and Fourier analysis II) you can take all new courses. If you have taken both Real analysis I and Fourier analysis I you cannot take Introduction to Real and Fourier Analysis (5 cr) If you have taken both Fourier analysis I and II you should not take Introduction to Real and Fourier Analysis (5 cr).

content.en:
General description: L^p spaces are some of the most fundamental function spaces in modern analysis. They are important on their own, and also serve as a basic building block for more complicated spaces, such as Sobolev spaces, which appear naturally in the theory of partial differential equations. The L^p spaces measure the integrability of the absolute value of a function f raised to the power p, and by doing so capture essential information on the size of the function. To study these spaces properly, and to apply their theory in practice, certain inequalities and approximation properties concerning L^p functions are essential. The first part of the course focuses on these spaces and the said properties. The goal of the theory of Fourier series is to represent a given periodic function as a sum of trigonometric polynomials. Trigonometric sums have natural physical interpretations and applications. For modern analysis it is very important to be able to represent relatively rough functions – not just continuous functions – in this way, and the above introduced L^p theory is central for this. Indeed, the theory of Fourier series has been an important motivation to develop modern real analysis. An introduction to Fourier series is given in this course. Fourier series are only useful for periodic functions. However, there is a certain continuous analog – the Fourier transform – which can be used in general. The Fourier transform e.g. has very natural interplay with differentiation and multiplication, and is a very useful tool in many mathematical problems, including those involving differential equations. The most fundamental properties of Fourier transform are developed using the L^p theory.

Specific contents:

1.Elementary real analysis (ca. 3 weeks) -L^p spaces (definition, completeness) -Convolution and approximation by smooth functions -Continuity of translations in L^p for finite p -Boundedness of the Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator

2.Elements of Fourier series (ca. 2 weeks) -Fourier coefficients (how and when they determine the function uniquely) -Dirichlet kernel and convergence results -Other summation summation kernels (Fejer/ Poisson) -(Discussion of L^2 theory will be brief, as this is included in Functional Analysis)

3.Fourier transform (2 weeks) -Definition and basic properties on L^1, interplay between differentiation and multiplication -Riemann-Lebesgue lemma, Fourier transform of Gaussians -Inverse Fourier-transform for functions with integrable Fourier transform -Plancherel’s theorem on L^2 Exercices are an integral part of the course, and crucial in explaining the wide range of applications.

outcomes.en:
The goal of the course is to introduce students to the design of practical mechanisms for the allocation of resources. The course combines theory and applications, with an emphasis on the latter. Upon successful completion of the course, students will be able to:

1) understand how different types of auctions work,

2) examine how resources are allocated when prices cannot be used, e.g., how to allocate kidney donors to transplantation patients,

3) apply tools from economics and game theory to the design of practical allocation mechanisms.

prerequisites.en: Recommended: TA3a Microeconomics I, TA3b Microeconomics II, and TA3c Game Theory
prerequisites.fi: Recommended: TA3a Microeconomics I, TA3b Microeconomics II, and TA3c Game Theory

content.en: The course is divided into three parts. In the first part, we study the concepts from game theory that are needed to understand market design and the functioning of auctions. These include the notions of dominating and dominated strategies, and the equilibrium analysis of games played under incomplete information. The second part of the course deals with auctions. We begin by examining the theoretical properties of the most common formats of auction. Then we study how auctions are run in several applications, including double auctions in financial markets and auctions used by Internet search engines to sell advertising. The final part of the course is devoted to matching markets. We study both two-sided and one-sided matching. In two-sided matching, there are two sets of agents—e.g., students and colleges—and each agent can be matched with only one agent of the other side. In one-sided matching, there is a set of agents and a set of indivisible objects—e.g., employees and office rooms—, and the goal is to match each agent with a distinct good. We study how to find optimal matches and examine their properties. Applications include kidney exchange, i.e., how to match donors with patients in kidney transplantation.

This course is given in Finnish, since it handles Finnish regulations and the course literature is in Finnish.
outcomes.fi: Kurssin tavoitteena on opettaa perustiedot ionisoivan säteilyn ominaisuuksista ja säteilyturvallisuudesta sekä maallikon että säteilyn käyttäjän kannalta. Ionisoivan säteilyn ja aineen vuorovaikutukset, säteilysuojelussa käytettävät suureet ja yksiköt, biologiset vaikutukset ja annoslaskennan perusteet esitellään. Ydinturvallisuuden periaatteet, ydinvoimaloiden ja ydinjätteen sekä toisaalta säteilyn lääketieteellinen käyttö ja ympäristön kannalta tärkeimmät säteilyuhat selostetaan. Säteilysuojelun keskeinen lainsäädäntö ja muut säännökset sekä annosrajoitukset käydään läpi. Säteilysuojelulaskuja harjoitellaan ja kurssiin liittyy pakolliset demonstraatiot umpilähteistä ja röntgenlaitteista. Kurssin riittävän hyvin suorittaneet saavat säteilyturvallisuusvastaavan (STV) todistuksen teollisuuden ja tutkimuksen säteilytoiminnassa osaamisalanaan umpilähde- ja röntgentoiminta sekä avolähteiden käyttö laboratoriossa säteilylähteiden luokassa 3.

content.en:
The goal of the course is to equip students with a toolbox of scientific research methods to benefit their future work in industry and academia, and to successfully plan and execute empirical studies for their Doctoral or Master's theses. The methods will cover the dimensions of qualitative vs. quantitative; subjective vs. objective, obtrusive vs. unobtrusive. They will be complemented with a set of strategies for assuring quality in empirical studies. 

The needs and interests of students from different majors and programmes (e.g. Information Networks, Software Engineering, Game Design and Development) will be met based on a diverse set of research examples and custom-tailored learning and exercise materials. 

Further specialisation courses are available for students who successfully completed this foundation course:

  • Research Methods: Case studies & Design Science (CS-E5011)
  • Research Methods: AI-based Data Synthesis & Analysis (CS-E5012)

outcomes.en: The aim of this course is to provide students with the fundamental concepts of modern solid-state theory, focusing on emergent phenomena in quantum materials. The course connects with a variety of concepts from previous courses of statistical physics, quantum mechanics and electromagnetism. The course especially emphasizes the importance of collective behavior, quasiparticles and emergent behavior in complex quantum systems.  Among others, the course presents the topological characterization of electronic systems, spontaneous symmetry and emergent quasiparticles, superconductivity, quantum spin liquids, fractional quantum Hall effect, tensor network and neural network quantum many-body algorithms and machine learning applied to quantum materials.

content.en:
Selected topics on quantum materials and quantum matter: topological insulators, superconductors and Majorana physics, quantum spin-liquids, symmetry broken states, tensor-networks and machine learning quantum materials.

List of lectures:
Lecture 1: Second quantization, mean-field and spontaneous symmetry breaking
Lecture 2: Symmetries, reciprocal space, Bloch’s theorem
Lecture 3: Band structure theory, tight binding and effective models
Lecture 5: Topological band structure theory
Lecture 6: Electrons in a magnetic field, quantum Hall effect and Landau Levels
Lecture 7: Superconductivity, Nambu representation and Majorana physics
Lecture 8: Magnetism, magnons, quantum magnetism and spinons
Lecture 4: Excitations and defects in quantum materials
Lecture 10: Tensor network and neural network many-body wavefunctions
Lecture 11: Machine learning for quantum materials
Lecture 12: Summary

outcomes.en:
After this course you will be able to explain why quantum mechanics is needed and know the theoretical basics of quantum mechanics.

You will be able to analyse a two-state quantum system and form the tensor product of multiple two-state systems. You will know the general features of time evolution in quantum mechanics and recognise the relevant equations.

You will be able to carry out calculations with both Dirac notation and wave mechanics. In particular, you will be able to solve simple problems in wave mechanics in one dimension.

Finally, you will be able to recognise solutions to systems with a central potential such as the hydrogen atom. You will be able to apply the probability interpretation to the wavefunctions which describe the electron of a hydrogen atom, and you will be familar with the concept of an orbital.

prerequisites.en:
Basic mathematical methods, especially linear algebra, matrices, and some familiarity with second-order ordinary differential equations.

High-school or early university-level physics, including (from classical mechanics) simple harmonic oscillators and the concept of conservation of energy.

It would be useful to have seen some quantum ideas, such as the uncertainty principle, the Bohr model of the atom and the idea of discrete spectral lines, before.

In addition (as outlined under the course prerequisites) this should not be the first physics course you take; it will help you a lot if you have already taken one or more of the basic courses.

content.en:
Fundamental postulates of quantum mechanics using a two-state system as an example, expressed in Dirac notation: state vectors, operators, measurement and the probability interpretation. Tensor products of multiple two-state systems. Quantum mechanical time evolution.

Wave mechanics in one dimension: simple one-dimensional potential wells and similar systems. The solutions of the three dimensional Schrödinger equation describing the electron of a Hydrogen atom.

additional.en:
Completion methods

A mixture of group participation, exercises and student self-assessment will be used to assess the course. There is no final exam. Alternatively the course can be completed by an examination.

Assessment practices and criteria

Grading scale is 0 (failed) - 1 (passed) - 5 (excellent)

Submitted exercises, group participation and other course activities will be taken into account as explained at the beginning of the course.

Activities and methods in support of learning

Weekly lectures, independent work by the student, weekly exercise sessions, which are partly done in calculation workshops in small groups, and partly independently.

The exercise sessions are returned to the assistant, who scores them. The total workload for the course is 135 hours.

Target groups

Course is optional within the programme, but compulsory within the Physics study track.

The course is available to the students of other programmes upon agreement with the teacher.

Teaching period when the course will be offered

Course is offered every year in period 2.

Recommended time or stage of studies for completion

Course is recommended for second year students of the Bachelor's programme in Science in the Physics study track.

Intermediate studies in physics

content.en:
The course focuses on the programming of quantum computers. The essence is to understand quantum software without diving deep into the complexities of the physics of quantum hardware. The approach is analogous to the fact that we can write software for classical computers without a detailed understanding of how transistors and other hardware components work.

The course starts with the operation of single qubit quantum gates and progresses further to deal with multiple qubits. In the end, we will investigate more complex quantum algorithms such as machine learning and optimization.

Programming assignments are mostly done in simulated environments using e.g. QisKit.

Because quantum programming is complicated in comparison to classical software, the main aim is to learn to read and understand the operation of small quantum programs.

We have visiting lectures from the quantum computing industry.

content.en:
Motivation: 

Quantum computing promises a technical revolution, but what exactly does it refer to? Popular science articles often talk about qubit, entanglement, algorithm, quantum chemistry and the discovery of new drugs and materials. It is important to introduce the foundations of quantum computing from a practical, realistic and (whenever possible) visual perspective. 

Quantum communication networks are already used for communicating across continents (Europe-Asia), and the first small scale quantum computers are available in the cloud for experiments.  

Nevertheless, industrially relevant quantum computing seems to be at least a decade away, because quantum error correction is a necessity, but the current hardware is too resource restricted.  

Students will write Python scripts that will simulate, compile and optimize quantum circuits. Attendees will be able to follow the latest technical news and evaluate their importance. Additionally, participants will have the opportunity to carry out small exploratory research projects related to the topics presented.

content.en:
TU-L0031 provides an overview of qualitative research methods that are commonly used in management research. Different approaches include case studies, action research, ethnography, and historical analysis. We will look at the steps involved in planning a research project, data collection and analysis, and reporting (i.e. writing up) in a way that is expected for publication in top management journals.

TU-L0031 is an interactive class with learning based predominantly on class discussions and activities.  Students are expected to properly prepare for each class, attend class, and actively participate in daily activities and discussions.

 

This is a compulsory course for the students in the field of IEM and an optional course for the Doctoral Program in Science. The course is open to other Aalto University doctoral students (i.e. from Aalto BIZ) and students from other universities as long as the class size permits.

content.en:
The physical foundations and implementation of solid-state quantum electronics has attracted broad interest in the context of the realization of quantum information processing systems. In this course, we address the physics of superconducting quantum circuits and show how such circuits can be implemented based on superconducting thin films and nanostructures. We discuss the application of superconducting quantum circuits in quantum information processing systems and in quantum simulation. The following specific topics will be addressed:

  • Josephson effect and the Josephson junction as a circuit element
  • systematic quantization of a network of lumped-element electric components such as capacitors, inductors, and Josephson junctions
  • classical description of electromagnetics in one-dimension: voltage and current fields
  • quantum mechanics of one-dimensional transmission lines and resonators
  • cavity-qubit systems and the Jaynes Cummings model
  • operation of superconducting qubits: reset, quantum logic, and readout.

outcomes.en:
After the course, a student can:

  • Describe quantum condensed matter systems using a many-body Hamiltonian.
  • Derive correlation functions in linear response.
  • Calculate the electric conductance using the Kubo formula.
  • Use scattering theory to describe electron transport in mesoscopic conductors.
  • Use rate equations to characterize electron transport in systems with strong interactions.
  • Use equation-of-motion techniques to evaluate Green’s functions.
  • Use real-time and Matsubara Green’s functions to solve interacting many-body problems.
  • Evaluate Feynman rules for potential scattering and two-particle interactions.
  • Describe the excitations of an interacting many-body system in terms of quasi-particles.
  • Read and understand contemporary research in quantum condensed matter physics and use the acquired skills to solve current problems in the field.

content.en:
The course concerns applications of quantum field theory in condensed matter physics including equation-of-motion techniques for many-particle Green’s functions and Feynman diagrams for potential scattering and two-particle interactions. The interacting electron gas is of particular interest together with the transport properties of low-dimensional quantum systems such as quantum dots, nanowires, and other mesoscopic conductors. Several physical phenomena and methods are discussed, including optical and tunneling spectroscopy, Coulomb blockade, impurity scattering, and Fermi liquid theory. The course will prepare students for further advanced studies of quantum condensed matter physics, and it will bring them to the forefront of current research in the field.

The following topics will be discussed:

  • Second quantization & the electron gas
  • Time-dependence in quantum theory
  • Linear response theory
  • Transport in mesoscopic systems
  • Green's functions
  • Equation of motion theory
  • Transport in interacting mesoscopic systems
  • Imaginary-time Green's functions
  • Feynman diagrams and external potentials
  • Feynman diagrams and pair interactions
  • The interacting electron gas
  • Fermi liquid theory

The topics might slightly differ from year to year.

outcomes.en:
After completing the course the student

  1. Is familiar with the mathematical structure and postulates of quantum mechanics
  2. Can differentiate between the terms quantum-mechanical state and wavefunction
  3. Can build a quantum-mechanical Hamiltonian from the classical description of a physical system
  4. Can solve the eigenstates and eigenvalues of the Schrödinger equation in simple situations and knows how to generalize the computation to situations where analytical solution is challenging. 
  5. Can integrate the quantum evolution and the expectation values of physical quantities for simple systems.
  6. Can apply creation and annihilation operators to solve the eigenstates of a one-dimensional harmonic oscillator.
  7. Can apply the quantum formalism to model a qubit and a register of several qubits. 
  8. Can predict measurent probabilities from a given quantum state.
  9. Can apply perturbation theory to compute eigensolutions in a situation where analytical solutions is challenging.

outcomes.en:
The course is a master's-level class on advanced quantum mechanics, assuming some basic knowledge of quantum physics and mathematical tools such a linear algebra and complex analysis.

The course consists of lectures, exercises classes, and homework problems.

After the course, a student can:

  • Solve quantum mechanical problems using mathematical tools such the representation of physical observables by Hermitian operators and fundamental symmetries
  • Evaluate the time-evolution of a quantum system and the probabilities of specific measurement outcomes
  • Justify the electronic structure of basic atoms
  • Analyse composite quantum systems and entanglement
  • Describe the physical phenomena used to build quantum gates
  • Account for decoherence processes in basic systems
  • Predict the relativistic quantum behaviour of some particles
  • Explain the outcome of scattering experiments

outcomes.en: Upon completion of the Quantum Optics course, you will be able to analyze basic light-matter systems using operator methods, master equations, and standard cavity-QED models to effectively tackle eigenstate problems in quantum optics. You will understand how decoherence, noise, and dissipation enter quantum dynamics and how they shape the behavior of quantum systems. You will be able to compute and interpret photon statistics, correlation functions, and coherence measures, and distinguish classical from nonclassical states through experimentally accessible quantities. You will acquire basic knowledge of quantum measurements in discrete and continuous variables.

content.en:
The Quantum Optics course provides foundations to quantum light–matter interactions and quantum measurements in discrete and continuous variables. We learn how quantum optical states emerge and how interference, absorption, emission, photon statistics, noise, and decoherence are described within quantum physics. The course covers basic quantum models of light–matter interaction, including the Jaynes–Cummings and quantum Rabi Hamiltonians, master-equation approaches, and the optical Bloch formalism. We explore how these principles lead to single-photon emission, controlled quantum gates, and the generation of squeezed and entangled states of light and matter. The course introduces central quantum-optical phenomena, including laser cooling, optical forces, cavity-QED effects, and Bose–Einstein condensation.

The course aims to build a strong conceptual and mathematical basis for further studies in quantum optics, photonics, and quantum technologies.

additional.en:
▪ Completion methods

The seminar will be organized close to the format of a scientific software engineering conference with peer-review practice.

Each participant writes a scientific paper (at least in the form and style) and submits it to the conference of the course. The paper will be peer-reviews by course staff and other seminar participants. In addition, everyone presents the paper as they would at a conference.

Participation in all sessions is compulsory, and any absence needs to be compensated as agreed with the course teacher.

▪ Assessment practices and criteria

The grade for the seminar is given based on the written paper (50%), presentation (30%), and reviews given to other students and activities in the course (20%).

▪ Activities and methods in support of learning

The main phases and deadlines will be announced in the first session. Details of activities depend on the number of participants and may thus vary yearly. If feasible, one-to-one feedback will be offered to each student.

Participation in all sessions is compulsory. The seminar sessions include lectures and discussions/workshops, e.g., paper writing and self-study material.

A suitable length of a seminar paper in this format is 6-10 pages.

Each presentation is 20 minutes (may vary depending on the number of participants). Think carefully about what to include and how much presentation material can be included. Each presentation is followed by a discussion in which all are expected to actively participate.

▪ Target groups

Computer Science Master students or doctoral researchers with software engineering as a part of their study plans.

▪ Teaching period when the course will be offered

Spring

▪ Recommended time or stage of studies for completion

Spring (Periods III–IV) of the first year, if starting the Master's thesis in Period III, or similarly according to the actual progress of studies.

▪ Study module

Software Engineering

▪ Expiry of studies

As usual

name.en: Quantitative methods in spatial economics D
name.fi: Quantitative methods in spatial economics D

outcomes.en: The course covers recent quantitative urban models that rationalize the observed spatial distribution of economic activity within cities. We will focus on two strands of methodological advances: (1) "equilibrium sorting" models that use properties of market equilibria to characterize preferences over locational amenities, and (2) "quantitative spatial equilibrium" models that can be used to undertake counterfactuals for general equilibrium impacts of empirically-realistic policy interventions. This entails: i) working with spatial data to generate the necessary model inputs; ii) setting, estimating, and inverting the primitives of the model; iii) using numerical procedures to solve for the spatial equilibrium and conduct counterfactual analysis.

  • AI to support coding
  • AI support for testing, debugging and quality assurance
  • AI-supported release processes
  • AI for project and process management, and for decision-making support
  • Industrial and societal impacts of AI for software engineering

additional.en:
Completion methods

Active participation in all course classroom sessions, or completing the required compensation for absence, online discussion, learning portfolio with reflection and assignments in Moodle, e.g., regarding own study design and peer-reviewing others' works.

This course can be arranged in a different format and with varying assessment methods for open university students.

Assessment practices and criteria

Grading is on a scale from 0 to 5.

The assessment practices are developed year to year, including written assignments about own study design and research methods, activity in sessions and peer-review of others' study designs. Details are explained at the beginning of the course.

Activities and teaching methods in support of learning

The course is being actively and continuously developed. The methods supporting learning are modified according to the feedback and experience from previous years.

Lectures are available as on-demand videos for viewing at the student's convenience. Online quizzes support the checking of understanding of the central topics of the study circle reading material and activate learners. Discussion in study circle sessions supports the development of collaborative skills and enhances understanding of the topics because of the need to arrive at a shared understanding. A short presentation helps crystallise one's research and practice presentation skills. Students will get feedback for their tasks (namely study design) in the assignments. The weekly schedule and deadlines for the assignments create a steady rhythm for the work.

Contents

The course consists of sessions in which the selected methods for conducting SE research are introduced (systematic literature survey, design science, case study, action research) and a study circle sessions in which the concept of validity and SE research from a methodological perspective are discussed in small groups based on the part of the course book and additional reading material.

The following describes the course as conducted earlier.

  • Content sessions (lectures) on the selected research methods.
  • Study circle sessions: reading the given material on one's own and discussion in groups during the study circle sessions)
  • Moodle workshops, e.g., on conducting defining Research Questions and Study Design.
  • Writing a Learning Portfolio, including reflections on own learning.
  • Articulation of validity issues in the domain of SE by writing concrete examples.
  • Defining the study design for one's thesis.
  • Short presentation of RQs and Study Design.
Target groups

The course is highly recommended to those who make their Master's thesis in Software Engineering.

Recommended time/stage of studies for completion:

  • In the second year of studies, the second period
  • Before or during the beginning of the Master's Thesis work

Term/teaching period when the course will be offered:

  • Second period

Active participation in all course classroom sessions, or completing the required compensation for absence, online discussion, learning portfolio with reflection and assignments in Moodle, e.g., regarding own study design and peer-reviewing others' works.

This course can be arranged in a different format and with varying assessment methods for open university students.

Assessment practices and criteria

Grading is on a scale from 0 to 5.

The assessment practices are developed year to year, including written assignments about own study design and research methods, activity in sessions and peer-review of others' study designs. Details are explained at the beginning of the course.

Activities and teaching methods in support of learning

The course is being actively and continuously developed. The methods supporting learning are modified according to the feedback and experience from previous years.

Lectures are available as on-demand videos for viewing at the student's convenience. Online quizzes support the checking of understanding of the central topics of the study circle reading material and activate learners. Discussion in study circle sessions supports the development of collaborative skills and enhances understanding of the topics because of the need to arrive at a shared understanding. content.en: The seminar focuses on contemporary topics in software engineering research and practice. Topics of seminar papers include those that are relevant to today’s software development practice and covered in recent scientific research. The seminar work can be based on literature, but searching for possibilities of investigating and reporting experiences or practices from real software companies or other development organisations is highly encouraged.

additional.en:
Literature

Basic material provided during the course. The literature to work on for one’s paper topic is to be searched from scientific databases; pointers will be provided.

Course completion methods

The seminar will be organized close to the format of a scientific software engineering conference with peer-review practice.

Each participant writes a scientific paper (at least in the form and style) and submits it to the conference of the course. The paper will be peer-reviews by course staff and other seminar participants. In addition, everyone presents the paper as they would at a conference.

Participation in all sessions is compulsory, and any absence needs to be compensated as agreed with the course teacher.

Assessment practices and criteria

The grade for the seminar is given based on the written paper (50%), presentation (30%), and reviews given to other students and activities in the course (20%).

Activities and teaching methods in support of learning

The main phases and deadlines will be announced in the first session. Details of activities depend on the number of participants and may thus vary yearly. If feasible, one-to-one feedback will be offered to each student.

Participation in all sessions is compulsory. The seminar sessions include lectures and discussions/workshops, e.g., paper writing and self-study material.

A suitable length of a seminar paper in this format is 6-10 pages.

Each presentation is 20 minutes (may vary depending on the number of participants). Think carefully about what to include and how much presentation material can be included. Each presentation is followed by a discussion in which all are expected to actively participate.

Target groups

Computer Science Master students or doctoral researchers with software engineering as a part of their study plans.

Teaching period when the course will be offered

The course will be offered each Fall, and a similar seminar on software engineering each Spring.

Recommended time/stage of studies for completion

Fall (Periods I–II) of the second year, if starting the Master's thesis in Period III, or similarly according to the actual progress of studies.

Study module

Software engineering.

Expiry of studies

As usual.

English.

outcomes.en: Students are able to search information related to a research topic, analyze information from different sources and write a scientific report in English. Students also improve their skills to carry out Master's thesis.
outcomes.fi:
Overall learning outcomes: Students are able to search information related to a research topic, analyse information from different sources and write a well-structured scientific report in English. These skills support carrying out a master's thesis.

Implementation specific learning outcomes:
- Engage with and synthesize interdisciplinary literature from HCI, design studies, feminist theory, and health-related research to develop well-informed scholarly arguments.
- Critically examine assumptions in health and health technology design using feminist, critical, and care-centered frameworks.
- Demonstrate an understanding of the concepts, methods, and frameworks covered to broaden design thinking for health-related challenges.
outcomes.sv: Students are able to search information related to a research topic, analyze information from different sources and write a scientific report in English. Students also improve their skills to carry out Master's thesis.

prerequisites.fi: Students are expected to have studied HCI, Health Informatics, Software Engineering, Interaction Design related courses as part of their master level studies. The aim is to prepare the students for their master's thesis work and academic writing.

content.fi:
The course considers the topic of designing technologies for health from a variety of alternative perspectives. Moving beyond traditional models, the course explores health as lived, situated, relational, and entangled with bodies, technologies, environments, and social structures. Through readings, discussions, and writing, the course encourages reflexive, inclusive, and ethically grounded approaches to designing technologies for diverse health experiences.

The course theme includes, but is not limited, to the following themes:
• Participatory and Co-Design Approaches
• Soma-aesthetic and Embodied Interaction Design
• Critical and Speculative Design in Health Contexts
• Feminist HCI and Care-Centered frameworks

outcomes.en:
After taking the course, the students will be able to

- Define soft condensed matter, explain how it differs from ordinary crystalline solids and isotropic liquids, give examples of typical soft matter systems and their characteristic physicochemical properties.

- Give examples of how physics is used to describe biological systems; summarize a scientific paper and present its core findings to others.

- Define, identify and give examples of colloidal matter; decribe typical features of colloids such as Brownian motion and Tyndall effect; describe different interparticle interactions acting between colloidal particles - especially van der Waals forces and electrostatic double layer forces

- Describe how physical properties, such as size and elasticity, of polymers are affected by molecular weight, temperature, and type of solvent; write a simple computational code to model the physical properties of polymers.

- Describe different experimental and theoretical methods for characterizing rheological properties of soft matter. More specifically, in the case of polymeric materials, the students will be able to explain how macroscopically observed viscoelastic behaviour is related to the molecular-scale structure and dynamics of the materials.   

- Explain the physical basis of surface tension, capillarity and wetting phenomena, and determine equilibrium states for given simple systems.

- Explain the thermodynamic and molecular-scale basis of the hydrophobic effect and molecular self-assembly, and describe the molecular-scale structural features of various self-assembled surfactant aggregates.

outcomes.en:
The main objective is to deepen and extend the learnings about selected central topics of the lecture course Software Architectures by independent study and hands-on work.

After the course a student can

  • Can apply basic analytical or simulation tools to estimate the impact of architectural decisions to a run-time characteristic of a software system
  • Apply architectural patterns and design principles in practice on a concrete design problem
  • Use a containerized production environment to deploy and run prototypes
  • Present technical work to peers as a poster or as a short video

In terms of generic and academic skills, students learn groupwork and interaction skills during pair working (optional). They also learn presentation skills needed for disseminating professional knowledge and experiences among peers. They develop further their systemic and strategic thinking by focusing on the design decisions of a service or application that affect their important qualities, including the inevitable trade-offs.

additional.en:
Completion methods

  1. Participation in teaching is the only way to complete the course. Completion requires the students to successfully finish all the tasks mandated as part of the course, including presentation of their results in a live poster session or a mini-seminar.
  2. This course may be arranged in a different format and with different assessment methods for open university students.
Assessment practices and criteria

There are three required tasks that all need to be completed:

  1. Report documenting the results (as required for the type of assignment)
  2. Poster presentation (common session for all, obligatory)
  3. Peer review of another students' work

In addition each student or group needs to attend a number of check point sessions with the instructor. The course is graded on a scale 0 to 5, where the quality of the report has the main weight (according to separately given criteria) and where a well-done peer review can compensate some deficiensis in the report.

Activities and methods in support of learning

Learning by doing is the main pedagogical driver for the course. Pair working (on voluntary basis) supports the development of co-operative skills and enhances understanding of the topics because of the need to develop a coherent solution for the assignment. Peer review done according to clearly stated criteria helps students to assess their level of learning and the quality of the exposition of the results. Doing the peer review helps also to focus on what is important in reporting technical results and can help improving own deliverable by comparison.

Obligatory check point meetings with the instructor helps to keep a steady pace in doing the work and helps to take corrective actions during the work, not just in the end.

Informal interaction with other students during the poster session creates a safe environment for presenting their own results to others.

Target groups

Optional course for all students of the Programme. Available also to students from other degree programmes. Suitable for exchange students if prerequisites are met.

tweetText.fi: Learn the role of Software Architecture in software development and fundamental architecture skills

outcomes.en:
After the course, a student:

Can explain what software architecture means, can explain its role in software development, and give examples of different approaches to leveraging software architecture. Can explain and demonstrate how architectural choices affect the qualities (a.k.a non-functional properties) of a software system. 

Can identify risks in a software development effort based on a description of its goals, project context, and constraints. Can make rational choices of architectural approaches in order to mitigage risks and to satisfy high priority quality requirements. 

Knows how to model software architectures using different views according to a canonical model structure. Can construct a model for a typical web-based application using UML and the canonical model structure. Can explain why architecture models and implementation tend to diverge in practice and what to do about it.

Can name and demonstrate (by examples) important general principles of software design. Can explain the key properties of the most important modern architectural styles and patterns and justify their usage in a certain context. Can apply common approaches (e.g. Domain-Driven-Design) for decomposing systems into sets of interacting components.

Knows what software frameworks are and can explain their distinctive features. Can explain the role of software architecture in product families.

Knows in principle how to evaluate the suitability of a software architecture for a system. Can give an overview of how to perform a software architecture assessment using an assessment method.

In terms of academic skills, students learn about software architecture as a possible career and as a path towards deep expertise in software. Students learn also groupwork and interaction skills during exercise sessions. They develop their systemic and strategic thinking by deliberately taking a system-level view to the required qualities of a service or application and the design decisions that affect those qualities, including the inevitable trade-offs between the qualities. The concepts of architectural styles and patterns also support the development of strategic thinking.

content.en: The course provides a broad but practical view of industrial software development. Students learn the main problems, models and methods of software engineering, including traditional and agile/lean software development. The main software engineering activities, including software requirements engineering, design, implementation, testing and deployment are covered. Supporting workflows, e.g. configuration management and project management are  also discussed. The course is delivered using moodle. Students pass the course by doing one moodle module each week, according to a fixed schedule. Each weekly module consists of a video lecture, a set of readings, a quiz, and a written assignment. After the course, students have a working understanding of software development in industry, and the necessary knowledge and skills to pursue further studies in software engineering.

tweetText.en: Learn test design techniques, system testing tools and the role of testing in software engineering
tweetText.fi: Learn test design techniques, system testing tools and the role of testing in software engineering
tweetText.sv: Learn test design techniques, system testing tools and the role of testing in software engineering

outcomes.en:
After the course a student:

Theme 1 - Testing in software lifecycle

  • Can explain what is the role of testing in quality assurance
  • Can place testing activities and levels within a software development process

Theme 2 - Test design & Test execution

  • Can select appropriate types of tests and test design techniques for a given software development context
  • Can apply common black-box and white-box test design techniques
  • Can use tools to automate test execution (unit tests and system tests)

Theme 3 - Management of testing

  • Can assist test leaders/project managers by identifying relevant testing objectives in a medium-sized application
  • Knows what kind of tools there are to help perform and manage testing
  • Knows the limits of testing and can help in selecting cost-effective ways of testing

In terms of generic and academic skills, students  develop their systemic and strategic thinking by considering the true needs of the stakeholders of a software systen and by transforming them into concrete and excecutable tests to validate and verify the fulfillment of central functional and quality requirements crucial for the success of the software.

additional.en:
Completion methods
  1. Participation in teachning: weekly lecture and exercises that are not compulsory but that yield course points (roughly a third of all available points). The exercises consists of an individual Quiz taken on-line and group work done in a face-to-face session. A small individual lab assignment may be included at the end of the course.
  2. The course can be passed by taking a separate exam after independent study of the course materials.
  3. This course may be arranged in a different format and with different assessment methods for open university students.
Assessment practices and criteria

The course is graded on the scale 0...5. 83% of course points yields grade 5 50% yields 1.

Part of the points needed to pass the course come from the exercises (15%) and the major part (70%) comes from the exam. The possible individual mini-project will also yield course points (15%).

Activities and methods in support of learning

Lectures present the topics to learn for each week. Students test their understanding of the central learning objectives by taking an on-line quiz that is designed to support learning instead of grading. The main learning event for the students is a weekly exercise session, where student apply the concepts and techniques while doing an assignment in small groups. At the end of each session the groups' results are reviewed and discussed together. The possible mini-project provides an opportunity to explore some topic in more depth according to individual preferences. The exam is an open book exam  providing an additional learning opportunity.

Target groups

Optional course for all students of the Programme. Available also to students from other degree programmes. Suitable for exchange students (if prerequisites met).

Every second spring in period IV

outcomes.fi:
Kurssin suoritettuasi

  • tunnet ohjelmistotuotantoprosessin vaiheet,
  • olet tietoinen vesiputousmallin ja ketterän ohjelmistotuotannon luonteesta,
  • osaat soveltaa versionhallintaa osana ohjelmistokehitystä,
  • osaat soveltaa UML-mallinnustekniikkaa vaatimusmäärittelyssä ja ohjelmiston suunnittelussa tarkoituksenmukaisella tavalla
  • tunnet ohjelmiston testauksen eri vaiheet
  • osaat soveltaa automatisoitua testausta yksinkertaisissa ohjelmistoprojekteissa
  • tunnet tärkeimpiä ohjelmiston suunnitteluperiaatteita ja osaa soveltaa niitä yksinkertaisissa projekteissa

prerequisites.fi: Esitietovaatimuksena ovat Ohjelmoinnin jatkokurssi , Tietokantojen perusteet, Tietokannat ja web-ohjelmointi tai vastaavat tiedot sekä Tietokone työvälineenä.

content.fi: Kurssilla tutustutaan eräisiin keskeisiin ohjelmistojen suunnitteluperiaatteisiin, ohjelmistotuotantoprosessin vaiheisiin, versionhallintaan, testaukseen sekä ohjelmiston rakenteen ja toiminnan mallintamiseen UML-kielen avulla. Opittua sovelletaan harjoitustyötä laadittaessa.

additional.fi:
Suoritustavat
Kurssiin kuuluu aloitusluento, harjoituksia ja harjoitustyö. Harjoituksia ja harjoitustyötä voidaan tehdä itsenäisesti, pienryhmässä tai opettajan ohjaamassa tilaisuudessa. 


Arviointimenetelmät ja -kriteerit 

Kurssin arvostelu perustuu harjoitustehtäviin ja harjoitustyöhön.

Arviointiasteikko on 1-5.


Oppimista tukevat aktiviteetit ja opetusmenetelmät

Opiskelja tutustuu kurssin aiheisiin perehtymällä itsenäisesti kurssimateriaaliin ja oheislukemistoon. Opiskelija syventää osaamistaan tekemällä harjoitustehtäviä sekä harjoitustyön, mitä tuetaan ohjatuilla harjoitustilaisuuksilla.


Kohderyhmä
Opintojakso sopii kaikille tietojenkäsittelytieteen opinnoista kiinnostuneille. Kurssilla opitaan erityisesti käytännön ohjelmistotuotannossa hyödyllisiä asioita.


Järjestämisajankohta opetusperiodin tarkkuudella
Kurssi järjestetään syyslukukaudella, periodissa 2 ja kevätlukukaudella periodissa 4.


Suositeltava suoritusajankohta tai -vaihe
Tietojenkäsittelytieteen kandiohjelman opiskelijat: Ensimmäisen opiskeluvuoden kevät, kurssien Ohjelmoinnin jatkokurssi, sekä Tietokantojen perusteet jälkeen.


Opintokokonaisuus
Tietojenkäsittelytieteen kandiohjelman aineopintokokonaisuuteen kuuluva kurssi.


Vanhentuminen
Normaalit säännöt.


Mahdolliset opetuskielet

outcomes.en:
After this course, you know how a radio transceiver is constructed. You understand how the practical receiver differs from the theoretical models. You know how to model a non-ideal transceiver and how to measure the errors produced by the non-ideal behavior of the transceiver.

You understand the structure of a software project and you are able to participate in a large software project with multiple programmers. You know the basics of problem solving methods and you are able to apply those methods in your own projects.

You understand what the interference is. You can predict how the interference impacts radio links and radio communication systems in general.
outcomes.fi:
Tunnet lähettimen ja vastaanottimen eri lohkojen toiminnat ja mahdolliset tietoliikennejärjestelmässä esiintyvät virhelähteet.

Ymmärrät ohjelmistoprojektin rakenteen ja pystyt osallistumaan ohjelmistoprojektiin, jossa on monta osapuolta. Tunnet systemaattisia ongelmaratkaisumalleja ja pystyt soveltaman niitä omissa projekteissasi.

Ymmärrät interferenssikäsitteen radiojärjestelmissä ja pystyt arvioimaan interferenssin vaikutusta radiolinkkeihin ja radioverkoihin.
outcomes.sv:
Den studerande lär sig känna till de olika blocken i en radiomottagare och -sändare, samt hur en mottagare i praktiken skiljer sig från de teoretiska modellerna. Den studerande lär sig modellering av en icke-ideal mottagare/sändare och att mäta felen som uppstår av dessa.

Den studerande förstår strukturen av ett mjukvaruprojekt och kan delta i ett stort mjukvaruprojekt med flera programmerare. Dessutom lär sig den studerande grunderna i problemlösningsmetoder och hur dessa kan tillämpas i egna projekt.

Den studerande förstår vad interferens är och kan uppskatta hur interferensen påverkar radiolänkar och radiokommunikationssystem i allmänhet.

prerequisites.fi: Suositellut esitiedot: ELEC-A7200 (suositellaan myös ELEC-C7230)
prerequisites.sv: Rekommenderade förkunskaper: ELEC-A7200 (även ELEC-C7230 rekommenderas)

content.en:
The course contains five laboratory works and an independent project. The laboratory works use software radios that are implanted by using the universal software radio platform (USRP) and GNU-radio framework.

During the course, the students study the performance of the software radio transceiver. They learn how the radio performance is described and how it is measured.

By using GNU-radio as an example, students learn how to structure a software project, how to handle version control and how to create and add new functions to the software based transceiver chain.
content.fi:
Kurssi koostuu viidestä laboratoriotyöstä ja yhdestä itsenäisestä projektista. Laboratoriotöissä luodaan oma radiolähetin ja -vastaanotin käyttämällä GNU-radio ohjelmistoympäristöä. Opiskelija tutustuu ohjelmistoympäristöihin, ohjelmistojen versiohallintaan sekä harjoittelee omien ohjelmistolohkojen luomista.

Itse rakennetun ohjelmistoradiojärjestelmän suorituskykyä selvitetään mittauksin ja testauksin. Samalla niin mittauslaitteet kuin eri ilmiöiden vaikutus radioyhteyksien suorituskykyyn tulee tutuksi.
content.sv:
Kursen består av fem laboratoriearbeten och ett självständigt projekt. Under laboratoriearbeten skapar den studerande sin egen mjukvaruradiosändare och -mottagare genom att använda sig av GNU-radio-programmiljön. Den studerande bekantar sig med olika programmiljöer, versionskontroll, och lär sig hur man skapar och tillägger nya funktioner till mjukvaran.

Den studerande mäter prestandan hos sin självbyggda mjukvaruradion, och samtidigt lär sig känna såväl mätverktyg som de fenomen som påverkar prestandan.

outcomes.fi:
Kurssin suoritettuasi

  • tunnet ohjelmistoprosessin, erityisesti ketterän prosessin vaiheet
  • osaat soveltaa ketterän vaatimustenhallinnan työkaluja (product backlog, sprint backlog, user story),
  • tunnistat tarpeen ohjelmistojen ominaisuuksien estimointiin ja tuntet joitakin menetelmiä sen suorittamiseen
  • osaat kertoa mitä ohjelmiston arkkitehtuurilla tarkoitetaan ja pystyt kuvailla tavanomaisimpia arkkitehtuurimalleja
  • tiedät miten arkkitehtuurisuunnittelu useimmiten tapahtuu ketterässä ohjelmistotuotannossa
  • hallitset ohjelmiston sisäisen ja ulkoisen laadun käsitteet sekä joukon validoinnin ja verifioinnin tekniikoita, joilla näitä pyritään turvaamaan
  • ymmärrät nopean tuotantosyklin edut, ja tunnet siihen tähtääviä teknologoita ja periaatteita (jatkuva integraatio ja tuotantoonvienti, tuotannossa tapahtuva testaaminen, DevOps)
  • osaat kuvailla mitä käsitteellä Lean tarkoitetaan ja miten sitä sovelletaan ohjelmistotuotantoon
  • osaat tunnistaa ohjelmistoprosessissa olevaa Lean-hukkaa
  • osaat toimia ympäristössä, jossa ohjelmistokehitys tapahtuu hallitusti ja toistettavalla tavalla

Kurssi harjaannuttaa erityisesti seuraavissa yleisissä akateemisista asiantuntijataidoissa:  tiedonhakutaidot ja tiedon kriittinen arviointi, kestävyys-, vastuullisuus- ja tulevaisuusajattelun kehittäminen, ajanhallinta, rakentavan vuorovaikutuksen taidot. sekä systeeminen ajattelu ja strategiset taidot.

prerequisites.fi: Esitietovaatimuksena on kurssi Tietokannat ja Web-ohjelmointi (TKT20019) tai vastaavat tiedot.

content.fi:
• Ohjelmistotuotannon historiaa

  • Ketterät menetelmät, erityisesti Scrum
  • Ohjelmistojen vaatimusmäärittely
  • Ketterän vaatimustenhallinnan työkalut (user stoty, backlog, A/B-testaus)
  • Ohjelmistojen arkkitehtuuri
  • Ohjelmistosuunnittelun periaatteita
  • Ohjelmistojen laadunhallintannan perusteet
  • Ohjelmiston testauksen menetelmät
  • Nopean tuotantosyklin mahdollistavat menetelmät (CI/CD, Devops, tuotannossa tapahtuva testaaminen)
  • Leanin sovelutaminen ohjelmistotuotantoon
  • Laajan skaalan ketterä- ja Lean-ohjelmistotuotanto

additional.fi:
Kohderyhmä

Kurssi sopii kaikille ohjelmistokehityksen prosessista kiinnostuneille opiskelijoille, joilla on riittävät ennakkotiedot.

  • Tietojenkäsittelytieteen aineopintojen pakollinen kurssi.
  • Avoin muiden koulutusohjelmien opiskelijoille.
  • Opintojakso voidaan tarjota osana jatkuvan oppimisen tarjontaa.

Suoritustavat

  • Kurssiin kuuluu luentoja, harjoituksia, harjoitustyö ja kirjallinen kuulustelu.
  • Harjoituksia voidaan tehdä itsenäisesti, pienryhmässä tai opettajan ohjaamassa tilaisuudessa. Osa harjoituksista on tietokoneella suoritettavia ohjelmointitehtäviä.
  • Harjoitustilaisuuksissa on läsnäolovelvollisuus silloin, kun tilaisuuden muoto edellyttää sitä.
  • Harjoitustyö tehdään pienryhmissä.

Vaihtoehtoisesti kurssin voi suorittaa erilliskokeella, jolloin siihen kuuluu ainoastaan kirjallinen kuulustelu. Tämä vaihtoehto ei ole tarjolla Avoimen yliopiston kautta. 

Avoimen yliopiston toteustavat voivat poiketa koulutusohjelman toteuksesta.

Arviointimenetelmät ja -kriteerit

Harjoitustehtävät, harjoitustyö ja kirjalliset kuulustelut otetaan arvioinnissa huomioon. Kuulusteluilla on suurin vaikutus arvosanaan, mutta hyväksytty suoritus edellyttää myös ennalta ilmoitetun vähimmäismäärän tehtyjä harjoitustehtäviä sekä harjoitustyön hyväksyttyä suorittamista.

Arviointiasteikko on 1-5.


Oppimista tukevat aktiviteetit ja opetusmenetelmät

Opiskelja tutustuu kurssin aiheisiin luennoilla ja perehtymällä itsenäisesti kurssimateriaaliin, oheislukemistoon ja esim. verkosta löytyvään lisämateriaaliin. Opiskelija syventää osaamistaan tekemällä muodoiltaan ja vaativuudeltaan vaihtelevia harjoitustehtäviä, mitä tuetaan ohjatuilla harjoitustilaisuuksilla.

Järjestämisajankohta opetusperiodin tarkkuudella
Kurssi järjestetään syyslukukaudella, periodissa 2.


Suositeltava suoritusajankohta tai -vaihe

outcomes.en:
Knowledge

After completing the course, the students will be able to explain in concrete detail what is needed for creating a functioning IoT prototype including hardware, embedded software, and network-based service. The students will be able to identify the key challenges related to embedded software development in the IoT context. 

Experience

After completing the course, the students will have an experience of an IoT concept design project from contextual study to hand-over of a design concept. They will also have experience in working in varying multidisciplinary teams in different roles in negotiating and describing technically oriented requirements.

Skills

After completing the course, the students will be able to plan and execute a multi-disciplinary concept design process for IoT products. They are able to evaluate also technical content of a requirements proposal.

outcomes.en: The course provides the skills to understand the computational methods used for Monte Carlo particle transport simulations. Monte Carlo codes are widely used as general-purpose calculation tools for particle and radiation transport applications in nuclear engineering, medical physics, fusion and space research. The course topics are focused on neutron transport and reactor physics, but the covered methods also apply to other radiation transport problems.

content.en: The course consists of five introductory lectures and programming exercises, during which the students gradually develop a simplified Monte Carlo transport calculation code. The exercise topics are related to collection of statistical results, geometry and tracking routines used in Monte Carlo codes, handling of particle interactions, etc. The exercises are recommended to be completed using a compiled language (FORTRAN, C, C++, etc.), since interpreted languages such as Python are slow when used for numerical simulations.

outcomes.en: After this course, you will know how to write computationally intensive C or C++ code that makes an efficient use of dozens of CPU cores. You will learn how to partition large-scale computations between multiple processor cores, and how to choose the best memory layout for your data structures. You will also get hands-on experience of offloading computations from CPUs to GPUs. You will learn new kinds of algorithm design techniques that are relevant in the context of parallel computers, and you will also learn which of these techniques actually work in practice on modern multicore CPUs and GPUs.

content.en: This is a practical hands-on course on algorithm engineering for modern parallel computers. The students will learn how to design programs that make the best possible use of the computing power of multicore CPUs and GPUs. The course projects will cover both numerical and combinatorial problems; the sole objective is to solve the task at hand in the shortest possible time. We will learn a whole range of techniques for speeding up computations, from bit manipulation hacks and special CPU instructions to high-level techniques such as choosing the right memory layout that makes the best possible use of the cache hierarchy.

content.en:
This introduction course will introduce you to relevant issues in cyber security. These issues include

  • the stakeholders' and users' ability to disrupt the functionality of a system
  • foundations of internet protocols
  • basics of cryptography
  • short history of malware and hacking
  • corporate responsibilities and liabilities, and
  • the never-ending software crisis that is related to the increasing amount of software and maintenance.

outcomes.en:
Modular forms are a central object in modern number theory, both analytic and algebraic. On the algebraic side, they played a pivotal role in Andrew Wiles’s famous proof of Fermat’s last theorem through their connection to elliptic curves. On the analytic side, they govern the distribution of arithmetic sequences such as prime numbers and the partition function. Modular forms appear also in many other areas such as algebraic topology, sphere packings, and string theory in physics.

A modular form is a holomorphic function on the complex upper half-plane that is symmetric under Möbius transformations of integer matrices. The aim of the course is to cover basics of modular forms including how they give rise to L-functions via Hecke operators.

prerequisites.en:
MAT21043 / MAST30143 Introduction to complex analysis

Introductory courses on basic number theory and Fourier analysis are also recommended.

content.en:
• Basic theory of modular forms
  • Congruence subgroups and the hyperbolic plane, fundamental domains
  • Hecke operators
  • Riemann ζ-function and L-functions: Euler product, analytic continuation, and functional equation
  • If time permits, we will explore connections to elliptic curves and automorphic forms

name.en: Business Model Canvas - Design your Company
name.sv: Business Model Canvas - Designa ditt företag

outcomes.en:
After completing this course, students will have learned about a growth mindset that is adaptable and resilient, essential for navigating the uncertainties of entrepreneurship. They will have learned about how to apply fundamental startup methodologies, differentiating between lean startup, effectuation, and causation approaches to business model creation. Students will also gain basic understanding of the Business Model Canvas and its nine interconnected building blocks. This includes basic ability to define and design compelling value propositions that are aligned with customer pain points and needs.

A key outcome is the student's ability to identify and segment target customers, develop detailed personas, and map customer journeys to create effective acquisition and retention strategies. They will be able to select on a basic level appropriate channels for communication and evaluate different revenue streams and pricing models. Furthermore, students will gain basic understanding of the internal infrastructure of a business, including key resources, activities, and partnerships, as well as cost structures. Finally, students learn the basic of how to implement customer-centric innovation through continuous market validation and adapt their business models to changing market conditions, allowing them to turn an idea into a scalable and repeatable business.

prerequisites.en: None.

content.en:
PROLOGUE

Chapter 1 – Introduction to business model design and development

Chapter 2 – Understanding Business Models

Chapter 3 – Business Model Design and The Business Model Canvas

Chapter 4 - Customer Segments

Chapter 5 – Value Propositions

Chapter 6 – Channels

Chapter 7 -Customer Relationships

Chapter 8 – Revenue Streams

Chapter 9 – Key Resources, Key Activities, and Key Partners

Chapter 10 – Cost Structure

Chapter 11 – Business Model Development and Agility

EPILOGUE

outcomes.en:
After successfully completing this course, the students will:

  1. Understand the basic concepts of optimization, implementation, and solution approaches.
  2. Formulate their ideas and decide which model is the most computationally efficient way.
  3. Recast their original model into LP, MILP, or convex models, if required.
  4. How to struggle with the operating and planning problems and make their model as solver-friendly as possible.
  5. Understand the basic concept of convex optimization, check the convexity of a model, and how to convexify a non-convex model.
  6. Consider the existing uncertainties in the model via stochastic or robust programming approaches.
  7. How to interpret the outcomes of the models.
