outcomes.en: The student masters the basics of continuous-time control theory and understands the principles and analysis methods of dynamical systems. She/he can design controllers by different methods and verify the operation of the closed loop system by analytical means and through simulation.
outcomes.fi: Opiskelija hallitsee jatkuva-aikaisen säätö- ja systeemiteorian alkeet. Hän ymmärtää dynaamisen järjestelmän perusperiaatteet ja analysointimenetelmät. Hän osaa analysoida yksinkertaisten järjestelmien dynaamista käyttäytymistä sekä osaa suunnitella erityyppisillä menetelmillä stabiloivan säätöratkaisun. Hän osaa simuloimalla tarkistaa suljetun systeemin käyttäytymisen.
outcomes.sv: Du behärskar reglering i kontinuerlig tid, regler-och systemteorins grunder. Du behärskar grundprinciperna och analysmetoder för dynamiska system. Du kan planera stabiliserande regulatorer med olika metoder och säkra det slutna systemets operation analytiskt och med simulering.

prerequisites.en: Recommended prerequisites: Basic knowledge of university level mathematics and physics. For example: Basic course of differential equations.
prerequisites.fi: Suositellut esitiedot: Yliopistomatematiikan ja fysiikan perustiedot. Esimerkiksi differentiaaliyhtälöiden peruskurssi.
prerequisites.sv: Rekommenderade förkunskaper: Grundkurser i matematik och fysik i universitetsnivå. T.ex. Grundkurs i differentialekvationer.

content.en: Fundamentals of analogue control. Dynamical systems. Frequency domain models. State space models. Design and analysis of control systems. The PID controller. Basic principles of digital control. In the exercises the Matlab/Control System Toolbox and Simulink are used.
content.fi: Säätö- ja systeemiteorian perusteet. Dynaamiset järjestelmät ja niiden käyttäytyminen. Siirtofunktiot ja taajuustason mallit. Tilamallit. PID-säädin. Säätäjien suunnittelu ja analyysi.   Dynaamisen takaisinkytketyn järjestelmän simulointi. Digitaalisäädön alkeet.  Harjoitustehtävissä käytetään Matlab/Control System Toolboxia sekä Simulinkiä.
content.sv: Grunder i analog reglering. Dynamiska system. Frekvensplanets modeller. Tillståndsmodeller. Planering och analys av regulatorer. PID regulator. Grunder i digital reglering. I övningarna används Matlab/Control System Toolbox och Simulink.

outcomes.en:
Knowledge
After completing the course, the students will be able to describe what activities are required for developing a design concept with functioning electronic prototype. They are able to outline what kinds of electronic and software components are needed for creating a functioning prototype. They will also be able to explain what kinds of tools are needed in the process.

Experience
After completing the course, the students will have an experience of a real collaborative project in creating a functioning electronic prototype. They will also have an experience in contextually grounding the idea and evaluation of their prototype as well as in presenting their design concept with a functioning electronic prototype. Furthermore, the students will have experience in producing documentation of their project.

Skills
After completing the course, the students are able to conduct a concept design project for creating electronic products by using a high-level prototyping platform. They will also be able to support their process with appropriate prototyping tools.

outcomes.en:
After finishing the Final Project in Digital Systems and Design, students have established deep theoretical and practical understanding of a research question related to Digital Systems and Design.

During the project, students gather practical experience, apply typical tools in the respective field and conduct research in the topic to generate novel outcome and results. The Final Project in Digital Systems and Design serves as a preparatory course to the BSc thesis and enables the students to build up competence and preliminary results required to successfully accomplish the BSc thesis.

outcomes.en:
After the field theory course, the student is able to explain electric and magnetic field quantities, electromagnetic waves, source quantities, and medium parameters, as well as the connections between these, using the differential forms of Maxwell's equations, medium equations, and the Lorentz force. The student is able to solve geometrically simple electromagnetic problems.

The student is able to model plane waves with time-harmonic complex vectors and solve propagation, attenuation, reflection, and transmission problems in various polarization situations using time-harmonic Maxwell's equations.

The student can explain the emergence of electromagnetic waves and factors affecting radio connections, and calculate simple parameters describing antennas.

The student can apply electromagnetic field theory in practical examples, such as in radio systems.

 

The boldface verbs indicate what activities are expected from the student during the course and what they are expected to be able to do after the course. The learning objectives are placed on the levels of comprehension (2/6) and applying (3/6) in Bloom's taxonomy which describes levels of competence.
outcomes.fi:
Kenttäteoria-kurssin jälkeen opiskelija osaa selittää sähkö- ja magneettikenttäsuureet, sähkömagneettiset aallot, lähdesuureet ja väliaineparametrit sekä näiden väliset yhteydet differentiaalimuotoisten Maxwellin yhtälöiden, väliaineyhtälöiden, ja Lorentzin voiman yhtälön avulla. Opiskelija osaa ratkaista geometrisesti yksinkertaisia sähkömagneettisia ongelmia. 

Opiskelija osaa mallintaa tasoaallot aikaharmonisilla kompleksivektoreilla ja ratkaista etenemis-, vaimenemis-, heijastus- ja läpäisytehtäviä erilaisissa polarisaatiotilanteissa aikaharmonisten Maxwellin yhtälöiden avulla.

Opiskelija osaa selittää sähkömagneettisten aaltojen syntymisen ja radioyhteyksiin vaikuttavia tekijöitä ja laskea yksinkertaisia antenneja kuvaavia parametreja. 

Opiskelija osaa soveltaa sähkömagneettista kenttäteoriaa käytännön esimerkeissä, kuten radiojärjestelmissä. 

 

Lihavoidut verbit osoittavat, mitä aktiviteetteja opiskelijan odotetaan tekevän kurssin aikana ja osaavan kurssin jälkeen. Osaamistavoitteet sijoittuvat osaamistasoja kuvaavan Bloomin taksonomian tasoille ymmärtäminen (2/6, comprehension) ja soveltaminen (3/6, applying).
outcomes.sv:
Efter kursen i elektromagnetisk fältteori kan du förklara elektriska och magnetiska fältstorheter, elektromagnetiska vågor, källstorheter och materialparametrar samt deras samband med hjälp av Maxwells ekvationer på differentialform, konstitutiva relationer och Lorentz-kraften. Du kan lösa geometriskt enkla elektromagnetiska problem.

Du kan modellera planvågor med tids-harmoniska komplexa vektorer och lösa problem med utbredning, dämpning, reflektion och transmission i olika polarisationssituationer med hjälp av Maxwells ekvationer i tids-harmonisk form.

Du kan förklara uppkomsten av elektromagnetiska vågor och faktorer som påverkar radiokommunikation och beräkna enkla parametrar som beskriver antenner.

Du kan tillämpa elektromagnetisk fältteori i praktiska exempel, som i radiosystem.

Verben i fet stil indikerar vilka aktiviteter som förväntas av studenten under kursen och vad studenten förväntas kunna efter kursen. Lärandemålen placeras på nivåerna förståelse (2/6, comprehension) och tillämpning (3/6, applying) i Blooms taxonomi som beskriver kunskapsnivåer.

content.en:
In future an electronics designer must have an understanding of a hardware-software interface and of restrictions a hardware can cause for softwares. Also a design methodology requires a good basic knowledge in programming, as programming is widely utilized in electronics design. On the course one becomes acquainted with a design process of an electronic device in a way, where modelling, simulation and finally controlling and operating system are connected to be one programmatic ensemble.

On the course a student develops his/her programming skills in a way which promotes hardware design and the course familiarizes the student with the powerful prorgammatic methods from an electronics design perspective. The course familiarizes the student with typical designing environments and different stages of the programmatic harware design from the modelling to the implementation are went through. The course provides to students an excellent starting point to improve their know-how in programming and in hardware design in their further studies.

content.sv: Beskrivningen av en position och en inriktning i tre dimensionen (3D). Framåt och inverterad kinematik av en robotarm. Beskrivningen av hastigheter och styrkor av en robotarm med en Jacobian-matris. Grunderna av robot dynamik och kontroll. Grunderna av rörelsemodeller för mobila robotar. Programmering av industrirobotar.

outcomes.en: After the course, the student is familiar with (1) the concept of a weakly and a strongly stationary process, (2) a sufficient condition for stationarity of an ARMA process, (3) how to built an ARMA model for time series data, how to estimate the parameters, test hypotheses, and forecast with the estimated ARMA model, (4) how to built a GARCH model for time series data, how to estimate the parameters, test hypotheses, and forecast conditional variance with the estimated GARCH model.

prerequisites.en: Bachelor studies in statistics. Recommended course MAT22015 Stochastic Processes.

content.en: The basic concepts in stationary time series analysis are introduced. Empirically most relevant autoregressive moving average (ARMA) model is studied in detail: its properties, model selection, estimation, testing and forecasting. The basic models for conditional heteroskedasticity particularly applied in empirical finance, their properties, model selection, estimation, testing, and forecasting are studied.

tweetText.en: Bifurcation theory: How to analyze differential equations if they cannot be solved

outcomes.en:
Bifurcations are changes between qualitatively different solutions we get from a dynamical system if we vary its parameters. Bifurcation theory is central for the general theory of differential equations and discrete-time maps; it is also the main tool for analysing mathematical models of real-life phenomena. This course is an introduction to bifurcation theory with emphasis on autonomous ordinary differential equations.

After successfully completing the course, the student will
- be familiar with the basic concepts of stability and of bifurcations
- master all one-parameter bifurcations of equilibria in continuous-time dynamical systems
- understand 2-dimensional systems exhaustively with extensions to higher dimensions
- have a solid basis for further studies in bifurcation theory

prerequisites.en: Differentiaaliyhtälöt I-II (MAT21012 and MAT21013) or BSMA2007 Differential equations or an equivalent course on differential equations (must include homogeneous linear systems of ordinary differential equations).

content.en:
- Continuous- and discrete-time nonlinear dynamical systems
- Equilibria and stability: Linearization and the Hartman-Grobman theorem
- One-parameter bifurcations in one-dimensional systems: the fold and the period-doubling bifurcations
- One-parameter bifurcations of equilibria in continuous-time planar systems: the saddle-node bifurcation and the Hopf bifurcation
- Periodic orbits, homoclinic and heteroclinic orbits, and the Poincare-Bendixson theorem
- Extension to multidimensional continuous-time systems: the center manifold
- Poincare maps and bifurcations of limit cycles
- A brief outlook on two-parameter bifurcations

outcomes.en:
Complex dynamics is a part of two fields, dynamical systems and complex analysis. With tools from complex analysis one obtains a surprisingly detailed understanding of the dynamical systems arising from iterating complex polynomials. This also includes the geometry of the associated attractors or the Julia sets, the chaotic part of the dynamics. For analysis, complex dynamics allows fascinating applications and results of the field.

In brief, the aim of the course is to understand these questions mathematically, both the local dynamics and, in particular, the geometry of Julia sets and the Mandelbrot set.

outcomes.en:
The main goals of the course:

1) Learn how the notions of being computable or being algorithmically solvable can be mathematically formalized in terms various models of computation such as partial recursive functions, Turing machines, register machines, and Post-systems,

2) Understand the meaning of the Church-Turing Thesis and the equivalence of various models of computation,

3) Learn the basic results based on Gödel numbering of programs such as the s-m-n theorem and the existence of universal programs,

4) Obtain basic understanding of decidable, partial decidable and undecidable problems,

5) Understand the basics of the theory of recursively enumerable sets,

6) Learn the basics of the theory of relative computability, reducibilities, and the degrees of unsolvability.

prerequisites.en: Introduction to logic II

content.en:
The birth of Computability Theory is marked by the works of Alonzo Church and Alan Turing in the first half of 1900's on how to rigorously define the intuitive notion of an effectively computable function. This course reviews several alternative ways in which this can be accomplished and the remarkable observation that they all give rise to the same formalized concept of a computable function on the natural numbers.

The course develops the basic theory of computability over the natural numbers. Then, using Gödel numbering of programs, the existence of universal programs and non-computable (undecidable) problems is established. The basics of partially decidable functions and recursively enumerable sets is also discussed. The last part of the course discusses the basics of reductions, relative computation, and degrees of unsolvability.

content.en:
Inverse problems is the scientific art of going from effect to cause.

For example, the “cause” can be a clear digital recording of a spoken message. The “effect” is a mumbled, noisy, incomprehensible sound signal coming through a bad communications line. Recovering the clean signal from the noisy measurement is an inverse problem.

Convolution is a linear operation widely used in signal and image processing, where it is often called “filtering.” It is a kind of a moving average weighted by a “convolution kernel.” In a discrete setting, convolution acts on one-dimensional data (vectors) or images (matrices). It is a model for imperfect measurements; for example a poorly focused photograph is a convolved version of a sharp photo, and in spectroscopy, crisp spectral lines are blurred by a device function. Convolution is also very popular in machine learning in the form of convolutional neural networks (CNN). The so-called Deep Learning is based on CNN’s and fast convolution operations implemented using graphics processing units (GPU).

Convolution is a useful tool in pure mathematics as well, especially in harmonic analysis and the study of partial differential equations.

The inverse problem related to convolution is called deconvolution. The observed data is interpreted as clean signal convolved with a kernel and corrupted with random noise. The goal of deconvolution is to reconstruct the clean signal from the noisy data. This is an ill-posed inverse problem, meaning that the solution is highly sensitive to modelling errors and measurement noise. Robust solution of deconvolution problems is based on regularization.

The course starts by introducing convolution for discrete signals and images. Naive deconvolution is attempted computationally using matrix inversion, only to find out that the ill-posedness of the inverse problem spells trouble for this simple approach. The source of the difficulties is identified using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), which will be introduced and discussed in detail in the course.

The difficulties can be overcome by a technique called “regularization.” Two regularized reconstruction methods are discussed both theoretically and computationally: truncated SVD and Tikhonov regularization.

Completion methods

The course has lectures, weekly exercises and an exam. It is possible to continue from this course to Inverse Problems Project Work course (5 credit units).


Recommended optional studies

Master's studies


Contents

Inverse problems is the scientific art of going from effect to cause.

 

In medical tomography, the “cause” is the X-ray attenuation coefficient inside a patient. The “effect” is a collection of X-ray images of the patient recorded along several directions of view. Recovering the inner structure of the patient from a set of noisy X-ray images is an inverse problem.

 

Mathematically, the X-ray images can be seen as a collection of line integrals of a non-negative function. Johann Radon proved in 1917 that a (reasonably regular) planar function can be reconstructed from the knowledge of its integrals along every line. This idea was refined and implemented by Hounsfield and Cormack in the 1960’s and 1970’s, resulting in modern CT scanners used in hospitals every day. And in Nobel Prizes for Hounsfield and Cormack.

 

Recently there has been growing interest in designing medical X-ray tomography that deliver a smaller radiation dose to the patient than the classical CT scanners. One way to do this is to take fewer X-ray images, but then the inverse problem becomes more ill-posed. Ill-posedness means that the solution is highly sensitive to modelling errors and measurement noise. Robust solution of limited-data tomography problems is based on regularization.

 

The same mathematical model appears in a variety of tomographic applications, not necessarily based on X-rays. Monitoring the ozone layer can be done tomgraphically using satellite-borne star occultation measurements. Electron microscopy can reveal the structure of molecules once a limited-angle tomography problem is solved in a regularised way. Secret chambers inside the Giza pyramids in Egypt have been found using tomographic imaging based on cosmic muon rays. Neutron tomography can be used for studying large metallic objects.

 

The course starts by showing how tomographic imaging problems can be modelled using matrices. First, naive reconstruction is attempted computationally using a least-squares solution. This fails because of the ill-posedness of the inverse problem. The source of the difficulties is identified using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD).

 

The difficulties can be overcome by regularization. Several regularized reconstruction methods are discussed both theoretically and computationally: truncated SVD, generalised Tikhonov regularization, Total Variation regularization, and wavelet-sparsity regularization.

tweetText.en: Spatial models in ecology and evolution: How to study spatial dynamics using a variety of mathematical methods

outcomes.en:
The goal of this course is to apply a range of different models and methods to study spatial population dynamics. The mathematical methods reviewed in the course include partial differential equations, bifurcation theory, mean field and pair approximations, methods developed for structured populations, and adaptive dynamics. By completing the course, the student will be able to

- construct and analyse reaction-diffusion models
- find travelling wave solutions
- analyse mechanisms leading to pattern formation
- construct and analyse patch occupancy models of single and multiple species
- construct and analyse pair approximations of population dynamics on regular lattices
- understand the principles behind spatially realistic models
- model large systems of coupled populations
- investigate the consequences of habitat loss
- gain insight into how evolution shapes spatial dynamics and how spatial structure influences evolution.

2. Patch occupancy models: the Levins metapopulation; competition-colonization trade-off; evolution of competitive ability; evolution of dispersal; kin competition
3. Lattice models: the contact process; invasion on a lattice; case studies of population dynamics and evolution on a lattice

outcomes.en: Missing data are common in many research problems, for example in health surveys. Missing data mechanisms are often selective, and simple complete-case analyses can yield biased results. This course introduces some commonly applied methods to handle missing data. After this course, students will be able to carry out statistical analysis of missing data using frequentist as well as Bayesian methods, and identify the type of missingness.

• need to handle missing data
• techniques to handle different types
• weighting
• multiple imputation

content.en:
Liberalisation of energy markets in many regions of the world has led to new electricity and gas markets with increasing exchanged volumes. Producers have than started trading energy and, especially after the financial crisis in 2007/2008, are subjected to regulations similar to those of the banking industry. Consequently, the modeling of physical assets, like hydro power plants or gas-fired power plants, is addressed using real option approaches borrowed from financial mathematics.


Besides energy companies, large consumers, banks participate in growing energy markets. Indeed, commodities are also increasingly recognized as an important asset class in fund management that can improve the portfolio risk profile. On the other hand, energy and commodity markets exhibit peculiar features and are based on different fundamentals that those of pure financial markets. Energy and commodity prices depend on physical constrains and are often seen as unstable and erratic. These facts of course, require proper and challenging mathematical modeling by risk management units and trading desks.


This course provides students with a good understanding of the stochastic methods of energy markets and equips them with the relative theoretical and computational skills. Thus, the course is suited for students who are willing to pursue successful careers as quantitative analysts, risk managers as well as traders in commodity trading houses, asset-backed energy companies and also in banks, insurances and consulting companies.

additional.en:
Timing
First Week

1. Stylized facts in energy markets. Basic contracts: day-head (spot) price, forward price, swaps. Overview of derivative contracts to model Physical Assets: calls/puts , Asians, spreads, swings, storages, weather derivatives. References: Chapters 1 and 2 of Eydeland and Wolyniec [5] and Chapter 1 in Burger et al [3].

2. Forward Models. References: Chapter 5 in Eydeland and Wolyniec [5] or Chapter 5 in Burger et al [3].

3. Exercises. Asian option Outright Power plans. Vorst Approximation. Discrete and continuous time.

Second Week

1. Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes. One factor spot models. Reference: Schwartz model [10], Lucia and Schwarz model [7], Chapter 4 of Eydeland and Wolyniec [5] or Chapter 5 in Burger et al [3].

2. Simulation of standard rv’s in Python. Reference: Glasserman [6].

3. Exercises. Pricing Asian options with Monte Carlo.

Third Week

1. Multi factors spot models. Schwarz and Schmidt model [11] and Regime switching models. Reference: Schwarz model [7], Chapter 4 of Eydeland and Wolyniec [5] or Chapter 5 in Burger et al [3].

2. Power Plants and spread options. Price sensitivities and approximation Methods. Margrage formula, Kirk approximation, moment matching. References: Chapter 8 Eydeland and Wolyniec [5].

3. Exercises. Pricing Spread Options. Monte Carlo and approximations.

Fourth Week

1. Lévy processes for energy markets. Compound Poisson process and Kou model. Properties of the Lévy measure. Construction of Lévy processes via subordination. References: Cont and Tankov [4] Chapters 3 and 4.

2. Gamma, Inverse Gaussian (IG), Variance Gamma (VG) and Normal Inverse Gaussian (NIG) processes. References: Cont and Tankov [4] Chapters 4.

3. Exercises. Calculation of the cumulants of the processes. Proof that any finite variation process is the difference of two subordinators.

Fifth Week

1. Lévy driven Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes. Naming convention, self-decomposability. Properties of the Lévy measure. References: Cont and Tankov Chapter 15 or Chapter 5 in Schoutens [9].

2. Gamma-OU, IG-OU and related processes. Mean-reverting Kou model.

3. Exercises. Simulation of Lévy and Lévy-driven OU processes.

Sixth Week

1. Calibration of Quoted options (Matteo Gardini).

2. Hawkes Processes. References: Rizoiu et al. [8]. andhttps://hawkeslib.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorial.html

3. Exercises. Weather Derivatives. Quantos and weather swaps and relation with the demand variation of sales contracts.

Seventh Week

1. American Options and LSMC model. References: Glassermann [6]

2. Swing options and Gas Storages. Keppo approach and LSMC. References: Bergeret al. [1] and Boogert and de Jong [2].

3. Exercises. Pricing an American put option with LSMC.

Other information

References:

[1] B. Berger, M. Dietricht, R. D¨ottling, P. Heider, and K. Spanderen. Semianalytical pricing and hedging of fixed and indexed energy swing contracts. Journal of Energy Markets, 11(4):1–26, 2018.
[2] A. Boogert and C. de Jong. Gas Storage Valuation Using a Monte Carlo Method. Journal of Derivatives, 15:81–91, 2008.
[3] M. Burger, B. Graeber, and G. Schindlmyer. Managing Energy Risk. A Practical
Guide for Risk Management in Power, Gas and Other Energy Markets. Wiley,
second edition, 2014.
[4] R. Cont and P. Tankov. Financial Modelling with Jump Processes. Chapman
and Hall, London, 2004.
[5] A. Eydeland and K. Wolyniek. Energy and Power Risk Management. Wiley
Finance, 2003.
[6] P. Glasserman. Monte Carlo Methods in Financial Engineering. Springer-Verlag New York, 2004.
[7] J.J. Lucia and E.S. Schwartz. Electricity prices and power derivatives: Evidence
from the nordic power exchange. Review of Derivatives Research, 5(1):5–50, Jan
2002.
[8] Marian-Andrei Rizoiu, Young Lee, Swapnil Mishra, and Lexing Xie. A tutorial
on hawkes processes for events in social media, 2017.
[9] W. Schoutens. L´evy Processes in Finance: Pricing Financial Derivatives. John
Wiley and Sons Inc, Chichester, 2003.
[10] P. Schwartz. The Stochastic Behaviour of Commodity Prices. The Journal of
Finance, 52(3):923–973, 1997.
[11] P. Schwartz and J.E. Smith. Short-term Variations and Long-term Dynamics in Commodity Prices. Management Science, 46(7):893–911, 2000.

content.en:
The courses SPM I and SPM II are both about the formulation and analysis of population models that cannot be properly described or analysed in a purely deterministic way because of the presence of noise.

In the present course, SPM I, we focus on environmental noise due to processes external to the population itself and that cause the population parameters to fluctuate in time. For the analysis of the models we use filter theory and stochastic differential equations.

(ii) identify the problems that can be answered using

density functions, and their relationships;

(iv) put a given problem in the light of different types of censoring and truncation; and

(v) argue when the existing survival methods are inadequate and hence, needs modifications.

tweetText.en: This course provides an exposition of some of the most central algorithmic approaches to solving computationally hard optimization problems in practice.

outcomes.en:
After successful completion the course, the student will be able to

-explain properties of and connections between decision, search, and optimization problems,

-give examples of polynomial-time solvable and NP-hard optimization problems,

-describe some tractable classes of NP-hard optimization problems,

-describe distinctive characteristics of exact and approximate optimization algorithms

-model optimization problems with linear constraints,

-solve linear programming instances by simulating the Simplex algorithm,

-explain linear programming duality,

-derive dual formulations of linear programs,

-derive different integer programming relaxations and cutting planes,

-simulate branch-and-bound and branch-and-cut search for integer programs,

-apply integer programming solvers to solve instances of NP-hard optimization problems by programming in practice,

-develop problem-specific optimization algorithms based on stochastic local search.

Assessment practices and criteria

Final grade is given by the percentage of points out of the maximum number of points available from the home assignment problems. Grading scale 0-5.

Activities and teaching methodsin support of learning

The course activities may vary per instantiation of the course.

The core study material consists of online lecture materials. Weekly lectures present the core study material with additional explanation and examples. Active participation in the lectures by the students is encouraged to support learning.

Students are given tutorial and homework problems geared towards learning the knowledge and skills described in the learning outcomes. Students discuss together solutions to weekly tutorials in person. Students submit individually solutions to mandatory homework assignments in electronic form (as instructed in the individual home assignment sheets) and discuss them with a teacher to obtain feedback. Both the tutorial and homework problems may range from theoretical problems to implementation-level tasks.

outcomes.en: Students will be introduced to and trained to use the tools to recognize convex optimization problems that arise in engineering, scince, economics. They will be introduced to the basic theory of such problems, concentrating on results that are useful in computation and engineering and computer science practice. The basic numerical optimization algorithms will be also practiced. Students will also be introduced to basic formats of convex optimization problems that are needed as an input form for convex optimization solvers, such as CVX, and will learn how to use convex optimization tools and existing solvers in their research.

tweetText.en: Learn transaction management and query optimisation algorithms  for databases
tweetText.fi: Learn transaction management and query optimisation algorithms for databases

outcomes.en:
After the course, a student:

* Know ACID properties for a transaction. Familiar with the transaction log.  * Know conflict serializability and view serializability. * Can use the precedence graph to test conflict serializability.  * Know two-Phase Locking on schedules.  * Understand the deadlock and deadlock prevention mechanisms.  * Know the timestamp protocol and the multi-version timestamp protocol. * Know write-ahead logging and shadow updates. * Know the recovery solution based on deferred updates and immediate updates. * Can use the ARIES recovery algorithm to construct the transaction table and dirty page table.   * Know sparse indexes and dense indexes. * Can construct the B-tree and B+-tree indexes. * Can construct the extendible hashing and linear hashing.   * Can transform a SQL query to a query plan. * Can estimate the costs of different query plans with indexes and join algorithms.

additional.en:
Completion methods

There will be lectures, study groups, and exercises. Attendance in study groups is required to attend the course exam. A separate exam can be taken with independent study, but the students need to submit the answers to all exercises and hands-on tasks before the examination.

Assessment practices and criteria

The course includes examinations, homework assignments, and study groups. A total of 100 points can be earned from the course's activities.

Renewal Exam:

The renewal exam can be taken only if the students submit the answers for all exercises and hands-on tasks.

Separate exams:

Separate exams do not require course participation. But the students are required to submit the answers for all exercises and hands-on tasks before the examination.

Activities and teaching methods in support of learning

The course consists of lectures, exercises, study groups, and an exam. 

  • Lectures: Attending lectures is not obligatory but it is useful. Lecture notes covering key facts will be posted on this page, but there will be additional examples and explanations during the lectures. We will also explain the answers to questions in self-assessment forms in lectures.
  • Exercises: The students should solve the problems at home and be prepared to present their solutions at the exercise session. The students are required to solve ALL problems. Give yourself as much time as possible to complete each assignment so you can complete it to the best of your ability and you don't have to rush or worry about incurring late submission penalties.
  • Study groups: The students read some material in advance and then discuss the material in groups during the meeting. Attending the study group meetings is mandatory. But if you have a reason (such as an emergency, personal illness, or others) for being absent, please let the lecturer know before the meeting.
  • Course exam: The exam covers the lectures (including self-assessment questions) and the exercises. No notes or other material is allowed in the exam.

content.en:
An AI agent is a program that can perform tasks autonomously on behalf of a user or another program. One critical question is how AI agents interact with the "real world", where the real world refers to both humans and the broader physical environment. From the perspective of the AI agent, the real world is a complex environment. This complexity imposes constraints on the extent to which the environment can be taken into account in designing AI agents that perform specific tasks.

In this course we explore how AI agents can be designed to deal with the interface between code and the real world to reliably achieve desired goals. The course approaches this topic from two angles:

  • Students will develop an idea into a concept or prototype of an AI agent that interacts with the real world
  • Students will explore theoretical concepts by delving into the literature and interact with companies

This course has been designed with a broad range of students in mind to get a mix of perspectives on designing and interacting with AI agents. Students will work in multidisciplinary teams.

  • have the ability to conduct a business analysis, make decisions and formulate recommendations or justify actions in a real environment.
  • have the ability to choose and apply relevant concepts/methods and/or tools and collect relevant data for conducting a business analysis and making decisions in a real environment.
  • have the ability to apply concepts, methods and tools pertaining to identifying and assessing the impact/value of a technology in an industry, market and/or organization and the innovation / business opportunities it creates.
  • have the ability to produce a professional writing on a business analysis topic.

content.en:
The course is composed by two components: 1) The online work part, where students will go through online content on assessing a technology and its business analysis; and 2) Group work part, where student teams work addressing a real-life business case for a partner company conducting the business analysis, providing recommendations and potential solutions. More specifically:

  • The (individual) online work includes three online modules: 1) Assessing the impact of technology; 2) Business research methodology; 3) How to make a market entry / grow on a new market. The online work is finalized with an   individual online assignment evaluated by the teacher, where you analyse in a brief report, current and future business potential technology, which can either be selected by you, based on your interest, or otherwise you can draft the report on the technology of the company case of your group work.
  • The group-work where students will work in teams of 4-5 students to prepare a group-report to address a business challenge based on a case offered by a company and the team-dynamics related to that process. Student is expected to implement a robust 4 steps business analysis consisting of: a) framing the business challenge; b) choosing appropriate business analysis tools; c) collecting data; and d) interpreting, critically discussing, making recommendations and finally reporting. 

Value elements of the I&E Study course are the following:

Interaction with a company: your goal is to tackle a company business challenge, make recommendation, and do your best to have an impact! This is neither an internship, nor a pre-recruitment.

Robust business analysis: you will develop your analytical skills on economic and social matters; you will learn more about how to handle a business analysis and make recommendations, using qualitative and/or quantitative research methods and reflecting upon the conditions for sound analysis.

Tech-based innovation: you will learn to employ analytical tools to assess the impact of a technology at a macro (industry, sector) or micro level (business, market).

outcomes.en:
The purpose of the course is to familiarize the students with opportunities, challenges, principles and tools of managing resources which are outside a firm's organizational boundaries for improved effectiveness, efficiency, and innovation. After passing the course the students knows what is the significance and strategic role of external resources in contemporary organizations and is capable of:

1) Designing and developing (purchasing) categories that support effective external resource management

3) Carrying out spend analysis and utilize it to support external resource management

4) Designing category strategies and choosing tactical sourcing levers that support the strategy

5) Executing total cost of ownership analysis and use it in external resource management

6) Executing supply market analysis for developing supply market intelligence (SMI)

7) Carrying out systematic sourcing process and preparing for contract negotiations

8) Using both competitive and collaborative incentives for managing suppliers

9) Leveraging external resources in innovation activities

10) Making systematic and justified make-or-buy decisions

11) Dealing with the specifics of public and service purchasing

12) Considering sustainability perspective in the management of external resources

The goal is to provide students both theoretical and conceptual tools to deeply understand the field, and the skills to solve the challenging problems in practice.

outcomes.en:
At the end of the course, the students can understand what Sustainable Development Goals are
and how they are structured and how to evaluate the business potential of an SDG target. The
students will learn about tools to evaluate net impact and stakeholder effects. The students will
learn about real life cases where companies have been successful in leveraging SDG-related
business opportunities. The students will learn tools to discover entrepreneurial opportunities in
SDGs and to map possible action steps to begin validating an SDG-related business idea.

content.en:
The course focuses on introducing the Sustainable Development Goals from a business
opportunity point of view, emphasizing possibilities for a new venture. In the course lectures, value
formation is evaluated from the point of view of stakeholder effects in addition to financial
performance, and assessed using tools that measure the net impact of a business. Various points
of views to corporate responsibility are discussed, and SDGs are presented as viable business
opportunities where the impact and profit potential of a new venture become indistinguishable.
Lectures address also actual entrepreneurial cases and opportunities related to SDGs, in particular
in the developing world. Case studies concern real life examples of successful SDG-related
ventures. Finally, the students will work in small teams to evaluate and ideate business
opportunities for a particular SDG target using startup ideation tools and techniques.

content.en: This course provides a deep dive into corporate venturing, exploring how established corporations participate in entrepreneurial activities and engage with startups through mechanisms such as corporate venture capital, venture building, and venture clienting. Students will learn about the strategic rationales, structures, processes, and outcomes of corporate venturing initiatives. The course adopts a blended learning approach, combining weekly pre-assignments (e.g., readings, online videos, and assignments), weekly in-class activities (e.g., case discussions and student team presentations), and hands-on project work.

outcomes.en:
During the course students develop their business judgment, teamwork, and presentations skills. More specifically, students learn to

(1) structure complex business problems analytically and evaluate the appropriateness of the chosen structure,

(2) generate strategic options as potential solutions for strategic situations; quantify the aspects of strategic challenge and the generated options; choose the appropriate options by evaluating the feasibility, quality, and potential of the options using several criteria; evaluate the quality of the options as well as the plausibility of the quantitative analysis, and reflect on the relevance of used evaluation criteria,

(3) explicate the assumptions associated with strategic analysis; identify, assess, and mitigate the risks associated with strategic plans; identify critical indicators to be monitored during the implementation of a chosen strategic option, and

(4) present a strategic analysis and recommendations in a coherent narrative form and evaluate the persuasiveness of the narrative.

content.en: Students solve Harvard-type business cases in groups of 3-5 students and present their recommendations to a jury. In addition, the students cultivate their own case solving process as individuals and as members of a group. The cases of the course focus on strategy formulation in various kinds of established organizations, typically assuming the viewpoint of a senior decision maker. Student groups act in a role that most resembles a team of management consultants.

  • Have the ability to reflect upon different materials and tasks in assignments and in contact teaching events
  • Can find their own role in group work among other students, and help own and other groups to learn

content.en:
The course covers the application of project management in different types of projects and in different organizations and industries. The course focuses on advanced project management approaches and methodologies in:

  • Organizing, scheduling and management of time in projects
  • Project strategy
  • Buying projects and subprojects
  • Contracts and different contractual arrangements in project business
  • Management of risk and uncertainty
  • Innovation in projects
  • Management of projects at the firm level, and management of project and business networks
  • Sustainability and responsibility in projects and project business

The project business framework is used for covering the distinctive and interconnected management areas of: management of a project, management of a project-based firm, management of a project network, and management of a business network.

content.en: The course introduces students to advanced concepts in strategic management and fosters their skills in strategic thinking, analysis, and decision making. The course focuses on technological and institutional changes that blur industry boundaries, give rise to new methods of competition, render existing business models obsolete, and change the competitive dynamics between firms. The concepts and frameworks discussed in the course help students understand, anticipate and manage such changes. Learning methods include in-class discussions, articles, individual and group assignments, and presentations.

  • Navigate responsible usage of AI in both academic work and corporate venturing contexts

content.en:
This course provides a deep dive into corporate venturing, exploring how established corporations participate in entrepreneurial activities and engage with startups through mechanisms such as corporate venture capital, venture building, and venture clienting. 

Students will learn about the strategic rationales, structures, processes, and outcomes of corporate venturing initiatives. The course adopts a blended learning approach, combining weekly pre-assignments (e.g., readings, online videos, and assignments), weekly in-class activities (e.g., case discussions and student team presentations), and hands-on project work.

content.en: The course provides an overview of the data analytics toolbox including topics such as causal inference, predictive analytics, optimization, and simulation. These topics are approached from two perspectives: 1) how can the analytics toolbox be applied to problems arising in operations management, strategic management, and organizational design and development; 2) what are the implications of increasing reliance on analytics for these fields. The lectures discuss how analytics relates to real-world problems while the weekly assignments provide an opportunity to gain hands-on experience in applying analytics methods. In the group project, the students work in teams to develop an analytics solution for a case organization.

content.en: Exploring the opportunity potential of deep tech can involve: A)Participating in Deep Dive is by individual application as an individual or as part of a pre-formed team. The experience is structured in three phases involving some combination of meetups, group work, independent study, reflective essays, reports and internships. The focus of the first phase is research commercialization fundamentals (1 ECTS) working on a case challenge for external projects. Students invited to participate in the second phase (2 ECTS) will need to deepen their understanding of the domain and the science involved working with the project owner. If a participant is chosen to work with the project directly as an intern, and additional 4 to 7 ECTS are available based on an agreement on scope and deliverables between Teacher in charge and the project owner, AND/OR B) undertaking an independent project whose content, deliverables and scope are agreed in advance with the Teacher in charge. The ECTS limit is 10 and participants must choose one point of exit for credit.

content.en: The focus is on a management and development of a modern technology-based business organization. The course includes lectures on high tech firms, relevant trends, business ecosystems and markets, organization and project management, new product and process development, entrepreneurial finance and human resource development. Special emphasis is on factors of a successful business-level digital transformation strategy and the related capabilities such as organizational change management. Lectures include insights from case studies of real-world business organizations, first-hand experiences from industry guest lecturers and might include site visits to industrial and business environments. The guest lecturers, content, and the case studies vary from year to year.

outcomes.en:
During the course you will learn to

  • Discover user needs and develop better understanding of what creates value for the customers, with
    • Robust and reliable interviewing approaches and techniques to discover (and reveal) needs, preferences and customer value
    • Startup-friendly methods to analyze the data and interpret the results
  • Test assumptions and product market fit fast, effectively and iteratively
  • Make data and customer research based decisions in building your first product in a strartup setting
  • Distinguish real needs & problems, that customers are willing to pay for solving, and lead to a genuine product market fit
  • Develop and test hypotheses about customer problem/solution, customer journey, buying roles & customer acquisition, business model & earnings logic, business/value ecosystem, etc.
  • Use different methods & frameworks, such as interviews, surveys, pitches, mockups, prototypes, and early product versions to validate assumption with near-zero investment

prerequisites.en: Minor in Industrial Engineering and Management, or similar, recommended.

content.en:
The value and growth of a startup is based on A) the value of the customer problem it is solving B) the usefulness of its product for this problem and C) its skill, speed, and luck in delivering that solution to a market. This course focuses on the very first steps of a startup that take place before there is a product (or a team/company). The course runs through the first steps of identifying and validating valuable user needs and then turning these opportunities towards a problem-solution-fit and minimum viable product (MVP).

This is a demanding, iterative, and unpredictable process, and product-wise, you need to nail three things simultaneously. You need to

  1. Find and focus on needs that are significant enough for the users to turn them into customer and common enough to form a market opportunity for scalable startup,
  2. Balance these choices against a developing business model and team, and
  3. Device early versions of the product to test and validate your learnings and your ability to build a solution.

You can grind it, you can hustle it, and you can try to force it with sheer will, but it’s probably more efficient and successful if you apply some skill to it.

content.en: The contents of the course is an understanding of growth hacking by doing in practice and learning the tools. The course starts with lectures and lessons about growth hacking tools and so-called hands-on sessions where the tools are taught (the tools and stack might change every year, but they will focus on search engine optimisation and management, as well as other relevant tools for digital marketing). Then after the first weeks the project work starts in which each teams gets a real client to work with. During the client work the teachers will hold sparring sessions with each team, and also there will be visiting lecturers to bring more examples and ideas about the growth hacking. The course ends with a gala in which each team presents their results.

Combination of theory and expert lectures, selected readings and online contents, and real world business case assignments from the following themes:

  • Digital and various high-tech markets and industries
  • Creative destruction, disruption, digitalization, convergence, automation, consumerization, commoditization, servitization, digital transformation; ecosystems, and platforms
  • Mobility, cloud (computing), social (media), information (analytics), big data, mydata, machine learning, artificial intelligence, data mining, blockchain etc.
  • Markets and industries, customer segmentation, business organization, entrepreneur, entrepreneurship process, venturing, leadership, management, business processes, operations, value creation logic and strategy
  • Opportunity identification, idea development, business model analysis and design, new venture creation
  • Ethical and sustainability viewpoints in business, case digital environment

content.en: TU-E3041 Leadership and Change Management is a course on leadership and its central task of accomplishing organizational change and implementing strategy. In the course, you will learn how leadership is connected to organizational change and about the implementation of organizational change initiatives. The course describes different aims of organizational change, organizational resistance to change, and the different sources of power and change mechanisms leaders can draw on to overcome obstacles and instill change in organizations. Furthermore, during the course, you will become familiar with various leadership and communication styles. You will learn when and how to adjust leadership styles to match different persons and situations. You will also gain knowledge about different types of challenges that managers and employees face during organizational change.

content.en: The course familiarizes the students with constructive and relational leadership theories and frameworks. Different approaches to leadership are critically examined by the students both separately through their own thinking and collectively in group discussions. These frameworks and their different aspects are utilized in analyzing and interpreting personal leadership experiences, and generic leadership related phenomena and practices. The course emphasizes the student's personal development through relational discourse, appreciative argumentation, and reflection. Towards the end of the course the students are expected to have constructed a personalized view on leadership and elaborated a preliminary plan of their personal development as a leader.

content.en: Expert entrepreneurs shape opportunities through the lens of their own means (passions, skills, networks), devise affordable loss experiments to test viability (prototyping), engage co-creators to shape the opportunity with them, and are open to the element of surprise. Discovering opportunities that are stimulating, "doable" and "worth doing" is a design driven process that is honed with practice. We will be iterating between divergence (exploring possibilities) and convergence (making choices) continually through the course. The group challenge is based on a contemporary issue that is both provocative and open to interpretation.

outcomes.en:
The main goal of the course is to help students become conversant in often difficult, complex and hard to grasp philosophical questions about identity, thinking, perception, the nature of the world we live in, methods and practices of inquiry and the nature of a good life.

More specifically, the course addresses themes related to overall philosophy, philosophy of language and the mind, epistemology and metaphysics, philosophy of science, ethics and applied philosophy. The goal is to give the students a grasp of a selection of central concepts and ideas in these fields to build a basis for carrying out philosophical thought in their everyday lives.

content.en:
Throughout the course, basic ideas and concepts of philosophical thinking are introduced and discussed. The emphasis is not on historical scholarship but rather in getting familiar with the conceptual tools needed to be able to practice and apply philosophical thinking in everyday life.

The course aims to:

  • Inspire philosophical thinking in everyday life.
  • Introduce conceptual tools and methods to practice philosophical thinking.
  • Introduce methods and criteria for evaluating thinking and argumentation.
  • Explore various opportunities to engage in philosophical thinking.

content.en:
Nearly all organizations exist to produce products (and services) that serve the needs of their users and customers. In doing so, organizations present significant variance in the ways the product management is organized and what type of functions, roles, and operations support the product management. Some of these ways are dictated by the external contingencies, some are just legacies from earlier days. Regardless of the origins, these ways are increasingly challenged by intensifying needs adapt to the changing needs of the markets. Finding and maintaining a fit between the customer needs, realities of production and development, and strategy and competition cuts through the whole organization.

The course starts from contemporary, user-centric product management, typical for digital service products, and proceeds to examine product management in varying settings, from digital to complex industrial settings. The purpose of the course is to examine the reasons and drivers for the different organizational and operational choices regarding product managent.

outcomes.en:
After the course, participants should have

  • Strengthened their proficiency in established and contemporary concepts, theories, and tools in strategic management of technology and innovation and their ability to apply those in real life,
  • Improved their analytical and prescriptive strategy skills, and
  • Deepened their understanding of different empirical phenomena in strategic management of technology and innovation.

Additionally, participants should have practiced

  • Analytical skills in defining and solving problems and reporting the results in academic manner
  • Reflection skills
  • Group management, coordination, and teamwork skills
  • Communication and presentation skills

This course will be particularly useful if you plan your careers as entrepreneurs, managers responsible for R&D, technology or innovation, or management consultants.

content.en: As the name states, the course is about strategic management of technology and innovation. It is not about individual technologies as such and takes a broad perspective to technology beyond digitalisation, including, for example, health and energy related technologies. Regarding innovation, course not only covers the ways how firms can profit and capture value, but also explores the concept of open innovation and ways of leveraging external sources. Relatedly, platform economy and its implications to strategic management of technology and innovation are studied extensively. Finally, while the dominating perspective on the course is the performance of a firm, the societal aspect and impacts for sustainability form an important part of the course.

content.en: The course is designed for engineering and design students who want to learn a societal perspective on technology. The course provides an overview of how the social sciences see the world, especially when it comes to technology and society. The course also sheds light on the social science methodology, namely how a variety of methods are used in social sciences to study technology, its design and development processes, use and broader societal implications. The course does not aim to convert students into social scientists, but rather intends to explain how engineering and design work is inherently societal, whether the engineer or designer acknowledges it or not.

outcomes.en: The aim of the course is to to develop participants thinking and analytical skills in various ethical issues related to digitalization and to to assume a critical attitude towards promises of moral improvement through digitalization; and to see digitalization and related technologies in their wider social, environmental and political contexts.
outcomes.fi: The aim of the course is to to develop participants thinking and analytical skills in various ethical issues related to digitalization and to to assume a critical attitude towards promises of moral improvement through digitalization; and to see digitalization and related technologies in their wider social, environmental and political contexts.

content.en: The course will pursue a cross-disciplinary investigation of the socio-ethical implications of digital technologies. We will combine theoretical viewpoints with concrete issues facing people who are implementing digital systems. We will cover a variety of themes, including data ownership and control, digital economics and surveillance capitalism, power and governance of algorithmic decision making, humanization of digital technology, ethics of robotics and autonomous systems and sustainablity of digital development in general.

  • discovering customer and user needs
  • customer value creation and customer value evaluation
  • linking RE with long-term planning and development
  • critical and creative thinking in RE
  • sustainability of digital services

outcomes.sv:
Students are able to search information related to a research topic, analyse information from different sources and write a scientific report in English. These skills support carrying out a master's thesis.

content.en:
The seminar focuses on cognitive, motivational, and emotional states and processes of software developers, and other human aspects of software engineering on the individual level. This includes, but is not limited to, the following themes:

  • Cognitive load and memory
  • Problem-solving and reasoning
  • Mental models and representations
  • Cognitive biases, heuristics, and decision-making
  • Comprehension of software artefacts (e.g., source code)
  • Methods for studying and measuring the above

The seminar will cover both classical and contemporary research articles on the seminar topic.

outcomes.en:
The goal of Artificial intelligence (AI) is the creation of more intelligent computer programs, to be used as is, or as parts of intelligent autonomous systems, or in automating society's increasingly complex infrastructure. An intelligent system must obtain data, understand it, reason about it, and make decisions based on it, and the complexity of this process requires tools that are quite different from conventional software technologies.

This course covers some of the core areas of AI that are needed in creating intelligent systems, including automated reasoning, automated decision-making, problem solving, and game playing.

After completing the course, you will be capable of choosing the right technologies for solving many types of hard problems requiring intelligence, have an understanding of how to implement them, and understand better the basis of AI and its relation to other information technologies.

outcomes.en: Once you have taken the course, you master the central concepts of computational complexity theory and are able to use these concepts to analyse the complexity of computational problems. You can formulate a concrete real-world computational task as a formal computational problem and formally reason about its computational complexity in comparison with well-known problems and complexity classes. You can use reductions and other complexity-theoretic concepts to identify which algorithmic tools such as randomisation, approximation, parameterisation and parallelism can and cannot help with the efficient solution of a given problem.

outcomes.en:
After this course the student is able to...

... design (and run) agent-based simulations to test hypotheses on how various microscopic social mechanisms lead to emergent macroscopic phenomena.

... understand the importance of thinking collective behavior and societies as complex systems with possibly emergent behaviour and non-linear phenomena.

... understand the pros and cons of large-scale social data from digital traces, and to analyse such data.

... use social networks as a tool for analysing social systems both empirically and theoretically and produce basic social network analysis results.

... identify ways of experimentation in CSS and explain why they are needed over observational data. In addition, they can construct simple large-scale CSS experiments given a research question. 

... identify various challenges related to ethics, privacy and reproducibility is CSS and assess privacy risks related to social data, and appreciate the importance of these aspects of CSS.

content.en:
Computational techniques have revolutionised social sciences leading to the fast-growing field of computational social science. While until recently it was only possible to use small-scale questionnaires studies and aggregated statistics to probe peoples’ lives, we can now have access to detailed logs of behavior of millions of people via the digital traces they leave in social media, mobile phones and other electronic means. Similarly, instead of theoretising how the different micro-scale behavioral patterns we observe in the data affects the macro-scale society using thought experiments and simplified models, we can now perform massive computer simulations to search for such emergent phenomena. In recent years, such techniques have been both used to test long-standing theories in social science but also to come up with completely new kinds of understanding of societies and individual behavior patterns. In addition to scientific research, social media platforms, game companies, online retailers and many other types of companies are using these techniques more and more to gain insight on their users behavior and competitive advantage. These analyses require a combination of techniques and ideas from computer science, applied mathematics and social sciences.

In this course you will learn basic techniques and ideas of computational social science with the emphasis on computation. You will learn how to analyse data on detailed behavior of millions of people and draw conclusions on the system level behavior that emerges from it. You will build simulations of artificial societies, and see how various societal phenomena, such as segregation, inequality and polarisation, can emerge from individual behavior patterns that might seem relatively insignificant at first sight. Finally, as the ideas and techniques you learn are extremely powerful, we will discuss issues related to ethics and privacy in relation to computational social science research and practices.

Topics covered in this course include 1. agent-based simulations & artificial societes, 2. digital footprints and social data, 3. structure and dynamics of social networks,  4. experiments, and 5.  ethics & reproducibility & privacy.

outcomes.en: Having completed the course, you understand the security that commonly used cryptographic primitives provide as well as their limits. You can read and understand security definitions of cryptographic building blocks and are able to judge whether a cryptographic building block is suitable for use in a particular application, and you can assess security models for applications critically. You can construct reductions between cryptographic primitives and recognize whether small modifications to a cryptographic primitive compromise their security.

You can send a message at a low threshold before the course starts for determining whether you have the required pre-requisits, we are happy to help by giving a second opinion.

content.en:
We introduce cryptographic security models and concepts and understand the relations between them. We then apply the learnt concepts and techniques to real-world problems. In particular, we cover:

  • Pseudorandom functions/ciphers
  • symmetric encryption
  • asymmetric encryption
  • message authentication codes
  • signature schemes
  • selected advanced cryptographic primitives (might depend on the course instance), e.g., fully homomorphic encryption, cryptographic obfuscation, indistinguishability obfuscation
  • selected applications (might depend on the course instance), e.g., secure communication, attacks on TLS, secure distributed computation

outcomes.en: Once you have completed the course you have familiarized yourself with the art of declarative programming with constraint solvers, where the goal is to specify what is to be computed rather than how the actual computation is to take place. You will have an in-depth understanding of central logical representations deployed in the paradigm. Moreover, you are aware of the fundamental algorithmic ideas needed to implement constraint solver tools in practice. You will have a good understanding of some of the main applications of declarative and model-based solution methods, including analysis of discrete systems by state-space search and model-checking. The hands-on exercises ensure that you will gain practical modeling skills and substantial familiarity with application problems and their main characteristics.

content.en:
The course covers selected mainstream approaches to declarative programming with constraint solvers, such as Boolean satisfiability (SAT), constraint satisfaction problems (CSP) and satisfiability modulo theories (SMT), as well as some of their most important applications in computer-aided verification and validation of software and hardware systems.

In addition to some of the algorithmic technologies for constraint programming, the course acts as an introduction to declarative and model-based solution of hard computational problems. Application problems are solved by first representing the problem declaratively (as opposed to procedurally) in a high-level modeling language, and then finding one or more solutions by using a general-purpose solver for the high-level modeling language. The declarative models have a semantics separate from the solver algorithms, and the models can be used for multiple purposes and with different types of solver technologies. For example, the same model could be used for control and decision-making, diagnosis, and monitoring.

Specific contents are given on the MyCourses page of the course instance.

This course will give an overview of Gaussian processes in machine learning, and it provides both a theoretical and practical background for leveraging them. This is a more specialized course and assumes students already have a background in machine learning.

The goal of the course is to introduce the participants to scientific research approaches frequently used in technical fields and in the context of industry.

In addition, the course provides students practice on planning empirical studies using design science, case study, and action research approaches for their doctoral or master's theses.

The needs and interests of students from different majors and programmes (e.g. Information Networks, Software Engineering) will be met based on a diverse set of research examples and custom-tailored learning and exercise materials. 

Alternatives to this specialisation course:

  • Research Methods: AI-based Data Synthesis & Analysis.

One specialisation cannot necessarily substitute another as degree requirement, and students are consequently encouraged to check their desired course choice against the requirements of their respective major. The same holds if students wish to take multiple specialisation courses, and wonder whether the additional credits can be counted toward their study progress.

content.en: In the course the students work in a group on a real societal problem together with a real organisation looking into solving that problem. The course is divided into three parts. First is the preparation phase where the project context and metrics for success are defined, as well as the personal learning goals for each student. The second part of the course is an intensive design project in the end of which the team presents a service concept. The third part of the course is about reflecting and learning from the intense and realistic project setting.

prerequisites.en: Recommended prerequisites: There are no mandatory prerequisites for this course. However, students are recommended to have completed CS-E4340 Cryptography D and/or CS-E4370 Applied Cryptography D or otherwise have acquired solid background knowledge in cryptography. Highly ambitious students may also attend this course in parallel to CS-E4340 Cryptography D. Students are expected to be comfortable with mathematical reasoning, reading and writing formal definitions and proofs, and analysing behaviours of algorithms. Students with background knowledge in relevant areas (linear algebra, abstract algebra, number theory, theory of computation, algorithms, complexity theory, cyber security, etc.) will be able to strengthen and apply their knowledge in this course. The course is suitable for advanced bachelor, master, and doctoral students. We recommend the course especially for those interested in a bachelor or master thesis in the area of cryptography.

name.en: Special Course in Computer Science D: Algorithms and Society
name.fi: Special Course in Computer Science D: Algorithms and Society
name.sv: Special Course in Computer Science D: Algorithms and Society

outcomes.en: At the end of this course, you will be familiar with the fundamental approaches to, and challenges of, formalizing various decision problems that arise in modern society. You will know how to analyze and improve some of the most prominent systems designed to address these problems: democratic systems and AI systems. You will appreciate the opportunities and limitations of mathematical and computational approaches to societal problems and be prepared to communicate technical insights to nontechnical stakeholders.
outcomes.fi: At the end of this course, you will be familiar with the fundamental approaches to, and challenges of, formalizing various decision problems that arise in modern society. You will know how to analyze and improve some of the most prominent systems designed to address these problems: democratic systems and AI systems. You will appreciate the opportunities and limitations of mathematical and computational approaches to societal problems and be prepared to communicate technical insights to nontechnical stakeholders.

prerequisites.en:
Mathematical maturity (the ability to follow and write mathematical proofs).
Basic understanding of algorithms, discrete structures, statistics, probability theory, and machine learning.
prerequisites.fi:
Mathematical maturity (the ability to follow and write mathematical proofs).
Basic understanding of algorithms, discrete structures, statistics, probability theory, and machine learning.

content.en: In this course, we will explore both the algorithmic foundations of society and the societal foundations of algorithms, from a mathematical and computational perspective. We will analyze the algorithms underlying democratic processes, such as mechanisms for taking collective decisions (computational social choice), assigning seats in representative assemblies (apportionment), or allocating shared resources (fair division); study the computational properties of democratic innovations (e.g., sortition and liquid democracy); and examine different formalizations of features commonly demanded from algorithmic systems, especially in the context of Responsible AI (such as fairness and explainability). The joint treatment of algorithms deployed by society and algorithms deployed in society will allow us to expose their shared cross-cutting concerns, and it will demonstrate how combining mathematical formalization and computational thinking with concepts and insights from the social sciences can help us frame and address important real-world challenges.

  • Apply Do-Calculus Principles: Use do-calculus to estimate causal effects and adjust for confounding variables in causal models.
  • Understand Counterfactual Reasoning: Formulate and evaluate counterfactuals to answer “what-if” questions.

content.en:
“Correlation does not imply causation”: most statistics courses focus on the former. However, understanding cause–effect relationships is crucial to making decisions such as whether a drug or an economic policy is effective or harmful. Causality is a central and widely-used concept in epidemiology, medicine, economics, and artificial intelligence.

In this special seminar, we will together read the book “Causal Inference in Statistics: A Primer” by Judea Pearl, Madelyn Glymour, and Nicholas P. Jewell and meet each week to discuss what we have read.

A preview version of the book can be obtained from https://bayes.cs.ucla.edu/PRIMER/.

tweetText.en: Differential equations: Learn the language of science

outcomes.en:
The course covers the basic theory of ordinary differential equations using a lively and modern approach, which combines mathematical theory with real-life applications. After successfully completing the course, the student will be able to

  • solve important types of first-order differential equations (separable, linear, homogeneous, Bernoulli)
  • solve second-order differential equations (linear with constant coefficients, including nonhomogeneous equations solved with the method of undetermined coefficients)
  • understand an apply the Picard-Lindelöf theorem on the existence and uniqueness of solutions
  • use elements of the qualitative theory of autonomous equations (equilibria, stability, bifurcations) to investigate differential equations that cannot be solved
  • solve systems of homogeneous linear differential equations with constant coefficients
  • understand the concept of linearization and how homogeneous linear systems are used to analyze real-life models

prerequisites.en: A first course on linear algebra (matrices, eigenvalue-eigenvector), differential calculus, integral calculus (BSMA 1001, 1002, 1003 or equivalent)

content.en:
• Separable differential equations and growth-decay models
  • Linear equations, the use of integrating factors
  • Autonomous equations: equilibria, stability, bifurcations
  • Existence and uniqueness of solutions (Lipschitz continuity, Picard-Lindelöf theorem w/o proof)
  • Systems of linear differential equations, the principle of superposition
  • Linear equations of second order with constant coefficients
  • A brief outlook on the qualitative theory of autonomous nonlinear systems

name.fi: Elements of Hydrogen System and Storages D
name.sv: Elements of Hydrogen System and Storages D

outcomes.en:
After completing this course, the students are able to:

  1. classify and evaluate the technologies in the hydrogen value chain that aim to decarbonize the power and energy sector, industrial processes, and end-users.​  
  2. model and conduct analyses on the functionality and societal impacts of the existing and emerging hydrogen technologies.​ 
  3. analyze and evaluate the role of hydrogen components at different stages of the value chain (production/conversion, transportation, storage, distribution, and utilization) and evaluate their behavior, connection, control, and synergies with the power and energy sector.​  
  4. apply the principles of capturing, storing, and usage of the products and byproducts of hydrogen in the hydrogen value chain.​ 
  5. analyze and develop the components and feasible technical solutions for optimal operation and planning of the power and energy sector.
  6. identify, create, and push forward new business opportunities related to hydrogen technologies. ​ 
  7. manage uncertainties when dealing with challenges in future energy technologies.  
  8. know how to analyze the dynamic and steady-state behavior of the existing and upcoming components.

content.en:
The basic elements of the hydrogen systems will all be given with a detailed introduction of their operation principle, including:

  1. electrolysers which convert renewables into green hydrogen
  2. tubework and H2 transportation − how to transport hydrogen safely?
  3. H2 storage − how to store hydrogen for later usage?
  4. Compressors − how to compress hydrogen for safe usage?
  5. H2 tubework physics and dynamic phenomena − the basic operation principle of hydrogen transportation.
  6. material questions − the basic materials needed for the hydrogen system.
  7. safety questions – how to guarantee the safety of the hydrogen system during all the processes?
  8. H2 use cases and their influence on H2 tubework: how does the usage of hydrogen affect hydrogen transportation?
  9. integration of the power system and hydrogen system. Demand of flexibility (power/demand balance), sources of flexibility, integrated system dynamics − this section will give a special focus on describing how hydrogen energy will affect the holistic energy systems.
